atoms.effect: The occupant's lawful tenancy continues under its existing terms from the date the landlord gave actual written notice until the notice period expires, notwithstanding the lease. This moves the tenancy end date and so the rent owed and the deposit clock.
atoms.quote: If the landlord fails to provide timely notice, the occupant's lawful tenancy shall continue under the existing terms of the tenancy from the date on which the landlord gave actual written notice until the notice period has expired, notwithstanding any provision of a lease or other tenancy agreement to the contrary.
atoms.cross_time: Two versions in the saved text (NB effective 2024-08-18 until 2034-06-15; NB effective 2034-06-15). The quoted sentence is in both.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: 226-c notice is required.
atoms.effect: Notice length depends on the longer of cumulative occupancy or lease term: under 1 year and lease under 1 year: at least 30 days; 1-2 years: at least 60 days; over 2 years or lease of 2+ years: at least 90 days.
atoms.quote: (b) If the tenant has occupied the unit for less than one year and does not have a lease term of at least one year, the landlord shall provide at least thirty days' notice. (c) If the tenant has occupied the unit for more than one year but less than two years, or has a lease term of at least one year but less than two years, the landlord shall provide at least sixty days' notice. (d) If the tenant has occupied the unit for more than two years or has a lease term of at least two years, the landlord shall provide at least ninety days' notice.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: The building is destroyed or physically injured by a sudden, unexpected cause (fire, storm, collapse, flood or a kindred casualty), the injury leaves it untenantable and unfit for occupancy, without the tenant's fault, and no written agreement provides otherwise; the tenant quits and surrenders. Gradual wear and decay is outside the section (the lease and NY:RPL-235-b govern it).
atoms.effect: Tenant owes no rent after surrender; rent paid in advance or accrued is adjusted to the surrender date.
judgment_terms: without his or her fault or neglect
atoms.quote: he or she is not liable to pay to the lessor or owner, rent for the time subsequent to the surrender. Any rent paid in advance or which may have accrued by the terms of a lease or any other hiring shall be adjusted to the date of such surrender.

construction.quote: The leaking was not caused by any sudden, unusual, or fortuitous circumstance, but seems to have been caused' by gradual wear and decay. The courts below held that the case was not within the statute, and that the lessee remained liable for the rent.
All that the statute requires in this respect is that the injury shall be of a physical nature and that the premises are thereby rendered untenantable and unfit for occupancy

atoms.reasoning: Suydam v Jackson (Commission of Appeals) confines the statute to injury from a sudden, fortuitous cause, not gradual decay; Warrin (1st Dept) requires physical injury rendering the premises untenantable. A vacate order for non-physical noncompliance falls under NY:ADJ-vacate-order-rent.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Tenant is 62+ (or turns 62 during the term) or has a disability (Exec. Law 292(21)), or is the spouse/dependent living with such person, and is certified unable to live independently and moving to a family member's residence, or has the opportunity to enter an adult care facility, residential health care facility, subsidized housing or senior/disabled housing project.
atoms.effect: Implied covenant: landlord must permit termination, release the tenant from rent for time after termination under 227-a(2), and adjust advance or accrued rent to the surrender date.
judgment_terms: certified by a physician as no longer able ... to live independently
atoms.quote: to terminate such lease or rental agreement and quit and surrender possession of the leasehold premises, and of the land so leased or occupied; and to release the lessee or tenant from any liability to pay to the lessor or owner, rent or other payments in lieu of rent for the time subsequent to the date of termination of such lease in accordance with subdivision two of this section; and to adjust to the date of surrender any rent or other payments made in advance or which have accrued by the terms of such lease or rental agreement.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Eligible tenant under 227-a(1) terminates.
atoms.effect: Written notice to the landlord or agent with the required documentation; effective no earlier than 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery; a mailed notice is deemed delivered 5 days after mailing.
atoms.quote: Such termination shall be effective no earlier than thirty days after the date on which the next rental payment subsequent to the date when such notice is delivered is due and payable.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Tenant lawfully terminated under 227-a; someone holds the tenant's belongings or interferes with their removal to enforce a claim for rent accruing after termination.
atoms.effect: Misdemeanor (up to 1 year and/or $1,000).
judgment_terms: for the purpose of subjecting ... property to a purported claim for rent
atoms.quote: Any person who shall knowingly seize, hold, or detain the personal effects, clothing, furniture or other property of any person who has lawfully terminated a lease or rental agreement covered by this section

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: A tenant or household member is a domestic violence victim (SSL 459-a) and reasonably fears remaining because of potential further violence.
atoms.effect: Tenant may terminate the lease and is released from rent after the termination date under 227-c(2).
judgment_terms: reasonably fears remaining in the leasehold premises
atoms.quote: such tenant shall be permitted to terminate such lease or rental agreement and quit and surrender possession of the leasehold premises and the land so leased or occupied pursuant to the provisions of this section and to be released from any liability to pay to the lessor or owner, rent or other payments in lieu of rent for the time subsequent to the date of termination of such lease in accordance with subdivision two of this section.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Tenant qualifying under 227-c(1) terminates.
atoms.effect: Written notice to landlord/agent and co-tenants (other than the perpetrator) stating the DV and inability to remain safely, with a termination date at least 30 days after delivery (first-class mail deemed delivered 5 days after mailing); documentation within 25 days.
atoms.quote: The notice shall specify the termination date which shall be no earlier than thirty days after such notice is delivered. If the notice is mailed via first class mail, it shall be deemed delivered five days after mailing.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Lease terminated under 227-c.
atoms.effect: Tenant pays rent pro rata to the termination date; landlord refunds prepaid rent or other payments for the period after the termination date, within ten days of delivery of the notice, provided the tenant has vacated.
atoms.quote: The tenant terminating the lease shall pay rent, pro-rata, up to the lease termination date pursuant to this section. (b) The tenant terminating the lease shall be entitled to a refund for any prepaid rent or other payments covering the period after the effective date of the lease termination, as long as the tenant has vacated the premises. Such refund shall be provided within ten days of delivery of the written notice as outlined in subdivision two of this section.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Tenant met 227-c(1) and gave proper notice.
atoms.effect: Defense to any landlord action for rent or breach-of-lease damages; no rent after the termination date. No defense to rent for the period before the tenant vacated and gave notice.
atoms.quote: shall have a defense in any action brought by a landlord against such tenant to recover rent and/or damages for breach of lease and shall not be liable for any rent after the effective termination date.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Lease terminated under 227-c.
atoms.effect: Landlord may withhold the deposit only as the lease or statute allows, and may not withhold any part because the tenant used the 227-c early termination.
atoms.quote: The lessor or owner may withhold a security deposit in part or in full to the extent allowed by the lease or statute, except for the early termination granted by this section, and shall not withhold any part of the security deposit due to the tenant's exercise of rights under this section.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: A terminating DV tenant has co-tenants on the lease.
atoms.effect: Landlord may not terminate or sever the co-tenancy without the remaining tenants' consent and must give them at least 30 days from the termination date to decide.
atoms.quote: the landlord shall not, except upon consent of such additional tenants, terminate or sever the co-tenancy. The landlord must provide the remaining tenant at least thirty days from the termination date to decide whether to consent to a termination or severance.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: landlord (and any agent it discloses to)
atoms.condition: Lease terminated under 227-c; landlord communicates with a prospective landlord or any third party (including a collector at hand-off).
atoms.effect: Must not describe or characterize the termination as an early termination; information about the termination and DV status is confidential absent written authorization or legal compulsion. What is furnished to a consumer reporting agency is outside this rule: FCRA 1681t(b)(1)(F) displaces state requirements on furnishing (US:15USC1681t(b)(1)(F)-furnisher-preemption), and the federal accuracy duty (US:15USC1681s-2(a)(1)(A)) already bars reporting a lawful 227-c termination as an early termination.
atoms.quote: the landlord shall not divulge, describe, or characterize the termination of the rental agreement as an early termination by a current lessor to a prospective lessor or any third party.

construction.quote: No requirement or prohibition may be imposed under the laws of any State—

atoms.reasoning: As to consumer reporting agencies the section is a state requirement on furnishing, displaced by 1681t(b)(1)(F); it governs communications to prospective landlords, collectors and other third parties.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Landlord knowingly or intentionally violates any part of 227-c.
atoms.effect: May be liable for liquidated damages up to $1,000, actual damages, costs and attorneys' fees; tenant waivers are void.
atoms.quote: Landlords who knowingly, or intentionally violate any part of this section may be liable for liquidated damages, not to exceed one thousand dollars, actual damages, costs and attorneys' fees.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: 2019-06-14 (L.2019 c.36 Part M s.4; immediate; applies to actions and proceedings commenced on or after)
atoms.condition: Tenant vacates in violation of the lease (early), residential premises.
atoms.effect: Landlord must, in good faith and according to its resources and abilities, take reasonable and customary actions to re-rent at fair market value or the agreed rate, whichever is lower. Once a new lease at that rate is in effect it terminates the old lease and mitigates damages recoverable from the departing tenant. The party seeking damages (the landlord) bears the burden of proof. Actual re-letting is not required to satisfy the duty (Toporek). It applies by the date the action is commenced (on or after 2019-06-14: Part M s.29), not by the lease date, so it covers a lease signed before 2019 when the landlord sues after that date.
judgment_terms: according to the landlord's resources and abilities
atoms.quote: if a tenant vacates a premises in violation of the terms of the lease, the landlord shall, in good faith and according to the landlord's resources and abilities, take reasonable and customary actions to rent the premises at fair market value or at the rate agreed to during the term of the tenancy, whichever is lower. If the landlord rents the premises at fair market value or at the rate agreed to during the term of the tenancy, the new tenant's lease shall, once in effect, terminate the previous tenant's lease and mitigate damages otherwise recoverable against the previous tenant because of such tenant's vacating the premises. The burden of proof shall be on the party seeking to recover damages.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: A lease provision exempts the landlord from the duty to mitigate.
atoms.effect: Void as contrary to public policy.
atoms.quote: Any provision in a lease that exempts a landlord's duty to mitigate damages under this section shall be void as contrary to public policy.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: A tenancy at will or by sufferance.
atoms.effect: Landlord may end it by written notice of at least 30 days, served by delivery to the tenant or a person of suitable age and discretion residing there, or by affixing if neither can be found.
atoms.quote: A tenancy at will or by sufferance, however created, may be terminated by a written notice of not less than thirty days given in behalf of the landlord, to the tenant, requiring him to remove from the premises

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Tenant gave notice of intention to quit at a stated time and does not deliver possession then.
atoms.effect: Tenant (or estate) owes double rent for as long as it stays, recoverable like the single rent.
atoms.quote: If a tenant gives notice of his intention to quit the premises held by him, and does not accordingly deliver up the possession thereof, at the time specified in such notice, he or his personal representatives must, so long as he continue in possession, pay to the landlord, his heirs or assigns, double the rent which he should otherwise have paid

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: Monthly or month-to-month residential tenant in NYC; landlord wants to end the tenancy.
atoms.effect: No removal for holding over unless the landlord gives notice under the 226-c(2) periods. The section binds only the landlord; the NYC tenant's termination is governed by NY:COMMONLAW-NYC-monthly-tenant-surrender and NY:ADJ-NYC-monthly-agreed-notice.
atoms.quote: No monthly tenant, or tenant from month to month, shall hereafter be removed from any lands or buildings in the city of New York on the grounds of holding over the tenant's term unless pursuant to the notice period required by subdivision two of section two hundred twenty-six-c of this article

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: Monthly or month-to-month tenancy outside NYC; tenant ends it.
atoms.effect: Outside NYC, a tenant must notify the landlord at least one month before the end of the term; no notice is needed to end a tenancy for a definite term. Residential landlords outside NYC use 226-c. The section does not apply in NYC (NY:COMMONLAW-NYC-monthly-tenant-surrender).
atoms.quote: A monthly tenancy or tenancy from month to month of any lands or buildings located outside of the city of New York may be terminated by the tenant or for a tenancy other than a residential tenancy the landlord, upon the tenant's or non-residential landlord's notifying the landlord or non-residential tenant at least one month before the expiration of the term of the tenant's election to terminate; provided, however, that no notification shall be necessary to terminate a tenancy for a definite term.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Tenant with a term longer than one month holds over; landlord accepts rent for a period after the term.
atoms.effect: Unless otherwise agreed, a month-to-month tenancy is created starting the day after the term expired. App. Term treats this as a renewal tenancy for HSTPA application (Case v 575 Classon).
judgment_terms: agreement either express or implied providing otherwise
atoms.quote: if the landlord shall accept rent for any period subsequent to the expiration of such term, then, unless an agreement either express or implied is made providing otherwise, the tenancy created by the acceptance of such rent shall be a tenancy from month to month commencing on the first day after the expiration of such term.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: A residential lease lets the landlord recover attorneys' fees/expenses (or treat them as additional rent) for the tenant's breach.
atoms.effect: An implied reciprocal covenant lets the tenant recover reasonable fees for the landlord's breach or for successfully defending the landlord's action. The landlord may not recover attorneys' fees on a default judgment. Waiver void. A clause letting the landlord recover attorneys' fees incurred in retaking possession after the tenant's default is within the section, so it triggers the tenant's reciprocal right.
atoms.quote: A landlord may not recover attorneys' fees upon a default judgment. Any waiver of this section shall be void as against public policy.

construction.quote: applies to a lease that authorizes the landlord to cancel the lease upon tenant’s default, repossess the premises and then collect attorneys’ fees incurred in retaking possession.

atoms.reasoning: Graham Court (Court of Appeals, 2015) reads RPL 234 to reach fee clauses tied to retaking possession.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: 2021-12-21 (L.2021 c.695 s.5-6, effective immediately); current wording, with the co-op shareholder carve-out, from L.2022 c.162 (signed 2022-03-18, effective as of 2021-12-21)
atoms.actor: owner, lessor or agent (including a manager)
atoms.condition: Charging a residential lessee (other than a co-op shareholder) any fee, surcharge or charge for legal services connected with the operation or rental of the unit.
atoms.effect: Prohibited unless the owner/agent has legal authority under a court order. 'Legal services' include court fees, legal representation, attorney fees, notary charges and administrative fees in managing the building, including court actions. Contrary agreements or assessments are void. So attorney or legal-admin fees cannot be put on the final statement or ledger without a court order.
judgment_terms: legal authority to do so pursuant to a court order
in connection with the operation or rental of a residential unit
atoms.quote: An owner, lessor or agent thereof shall be prohibited from assessing a lessee any fee, surcharge or other charges for legal services in connection with the operation or rental of a residential unit unless the owner, lessor or agent has the legal authority to do so pursuant to a court order.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: A court finds as a matter of law that a lease or clause (e.g., a move-out fee, liquidated damages or cleaning schedule) was unconscionable when made.
atoms.effect: The court may refuse to enforce it, enforce the rest, or limit it; parties may present evidence on setting, purpose and effect.
judgment_terms: unconscionable at the time it was made
atoms.quote: If the court as a matter of law finds a lease or any clause of the lease to have been unconscionable at the time it was made the court may refuse to enforce the lease, or it may enforce the remainder of the lease without the unconscionable clause, or it may so limit the application of any unconscionable clause as to avoid any unconscionable result.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: Rent (including arrears paid at or after move-out) is paid in cash or any instrument other than the tenant's personal check, or by personal check where the tenant asked in writing.
atoms.effect: Provide a written receipt with date, amount, premises and period, and signature and title of receiver: immediately if paid in person, within 15 days if paid indirectly. Keep cash receipt records for 3 years.
atoms.quote: Upon the receipt of the payment of rent for residential premises in the form of cash, or any instrument other than the personal check of the lessee, it shall be the duty of the lessor, or any agent of the lessor authorized to receive rent, to provide the lessee with a written receipt

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Rent payment method.
atoms.effect: Landlord may not require electronic billing/payment as the only method, nor charge a fee to a tenant who does not use it; waiver void.
atoms.quote: A landlord shall not require a lessee or tenant to use an electronic billing and/or payment system as the only method for the payment of rent. A landlord shall not assess any fee or other charge for a lessee or tenant that chooses not to use an electronic billing and/or payment system.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Landlord charges a tenant for reproducing keys to a single dwelling (e.g., unreturned keys at move-out, if billed as reproduction).
atoms.effect: Fee capped at 110% of actual reproduction cost, unless the tenant needed reproduction more than three times in a calendar year.
judgment_terms: whether a move-out lock/key charge is a fee 'for the reproduction of keys'
atoms.quote: A landlord shall not charge a tenant a fee for the reproduction of keys to a single dwelling greater than one hundred ten percent of the actual cost of reproduction

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Residential tenant dies; estate requests consent to assign or sublet, by registered or certified mail, with co-tenant/guarantor consent and assignee details.
atoms.effect: Landlord must answer within 30 days (after any 10-day information request) electing to terminate, consent or refuse; silence is consent. If the landlord terminates or unreasonably refuses, the lease is deemed terminated and the estate and other tenants are discharged as of the last day of the month in which the landlord had to act. Reasonable refusal keeps the lease in force.
atoms.quote: If the landlord terminates said lease or unreasonably refuses his consent, said lease shall be deemed terminated, and the estate of the deceased tenant and any other tenant thereunder shall be discharged from further liability thereunder as of the last day of the calendar month during which the landlord was required hereunder to exercise his option.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Residential tenant dies (lease made or renewed after enactment; not a proprietary lease).
atoms.effect: Estate may terminate on notice (registered/certified mail, with co-tenant/guarantor consent), effective when it notifies and surrenders possession. The estate stays liable for rent and debts before termination, including damage and expenses resulting directly from the death, but not for damages or penalties for inadequate notice.
judgment_terms: expenses the landlord may incur as a direct result of the tenant's death
atoms.quote: Nothing in this section shall be construed to relieve the tenant's estate of liability for rent money or any debt incurred prior to the date of termination of the lease, including damages to the premises and any expenses the landlord may incur as a direct result of the tenant's death, except that the tenant's estate shall not be liable for damages or any other penalty for breach of inadequate notice as a result of terminating a lease under this section.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: Residential unit; landlord charges for late payment of rent (including late fees carried into the final balance).
atoms.effect: No late fee unless rent is unpaid more than five days after the due date, and the fee may not exceed the lesser of $50 or 5% of the monthly rent (co-op shareholder carve-out).
atoms.quote: No landlord, lessor, sub-lessor or grantor may demand any payment, fee, or charge for the late payment of rent unless the payment of rent has not been made within five days of the date it was due, and such payment, fee, or charge shall not exceed fifty dollars or five percent of the monthly rent, whichever is less

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Tenant's rent check dishonored for insufficient funds.
atoms.effect: No charge unless the lease provides for it; then capped at the greater of actual costs or the GOL 5-328(3) amount ($20), with evidence of actual cost on request if above $20.
atoms.quote: a landlord, lessor, sub-lessor or grantor may demand any payment, fee, or charge from a tenant for the delivery of a dishonored check only if such payment, fee, or charge was provided for in the lease or contract between landlord, lessor, sub-lessor or grantor and the tenant

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: Lease provision waiving or limiting 238-a.
atoms.effect: Void.
atoms.quote: Any provision of a lease or contract waiving or limiting the provisions of this section shall be void as against public policy.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Rent paid by check (not money order, cashier's or certified check) is dishonored; the charge is in the lease per RPL 238-a(2-a).
atoms.effect: Landlord may collect the greater of actual costs or $20, providing evidence of actual costs on request when above $20.
atoms.quote: may if such instrument is dishonored charge or collect from the maker or drawer the amount of actual costs, charges or fees incurred by such landlord, lessor, sub-lessor or grantor for the return of such dishonored check or the amount set forth in paragraph (a) of this subdivision, whichever is greater

atoms.instrument: NY Military Law
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: tenant (entered military service after signing); landlord
atoms.condition: Dwelling lease executed by a person who later entered military service (or by that person's spouse), premises occupied by them or dependents.
atoms.effect: Tenant may terminate by written notice (mailing suffices). For monthly-rent leases, effective 30 days after the next rent due date after notice; otherwise the last day of the month after the notice month; unpaid rent before termination is prorated and advance rent after termination refunded. A court may modify on the landlord's pre-termination application. Overlaps federal SCRA 3955.
atoms.quote: Termination of any such lease providing for monthly payment of rent shall not be effective until thirty days after the first date on which the next rental payment is due and payable subsequent to the date when such notice is delivered or mailed.

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Deciding whether art. 29-H binds the landlord or its agent when collecting a former tenant's balance.
atoms.effect: Art. 29-H reaches a 'principal creditor' (to whom a consumer claim is owed, or its assignee for value) and its agent. A 'consumer claim' is a natural person's obligation, in or alleged to be in default, that arises from a transaction in which credit was offered or extended, primarily for personal, family or household purposes. A former tenant's rent, use and occupancy or damage balance under a lease is not a consumer claim (NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit).
judgment_terms: transaction wherein credit has been offered or extended
atoms.quote: "Consumer claim" means any obligation of a natural person for the payment of money or its equivalent which is or is alleged to be in default and which arises out of a transaction wherein credit has been offered or extended to a natural person, and the money, property or service which was the subject of the transaction was primarily for personal, family or household purposes.

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Identifying who art. 29-H binds.
atoms.effect: 'Principal creditor' is the person to whom the consumer claim is owed, or its assignee for value; a 'debt collection agency' collects debts owed to another or bought in default. A landlord's lease balance is not a consumer claim (NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit), so art. 29-H does not bind the landlord or its managing agent when collecting it.
atoms.quote: "Principal creditor" means any person, firm, corporation or organization to whom a consumer claim is owed, due or asserted to be due or owed, or any assignee for value of said person, firm, corporation or organization.

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Collecting a former tenant's consumer claim.
atoms.effect: May not knowingly collect, attempt to collect, or assert a right to any collection fee, attorney's fee, court cost or expense unless justly due and legally chargeable. Read with RPL 234-a (no legal fees without a court order).
atoms.quote: Knowingly collect, attempt to collect, or assert a right to any collection fee, attorney's fee, court cost or expense unless such changes are justly due and legally chargeable against the debtor

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Reporting or threatening to report a former tenant's balance.
atoms.effect: May not disclose or threaten to disclose credit-worthiness information known or with reason to be known false.
atoms.quote: Disclose or threaten to disclose information affecting the debtor's reputation for credit worthiness with knowledge or reason to know that the information is false

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Collecting a consumer claim before final judgment.
atoms.effect: May not communicate or threaten to communicate the claim to the debtor's employer before final judgment (except to execute a consented wage assignment).
atoms.quote: Communicate or threaten to communicate the nature of a consumer claim to the debtor's employer prior to obtaining final judgment against the debtor.

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: The tenant disputes the balance.
atoms.effect: May not disclose or threaten to disclose the debt's existence without disclosing that it is disputed.
atoms.quote: Disclose or threaten to disclose information concerning the existence of a debt known to be disputed by the debtor without disclosing that fact

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Communicating with the debtor or household about the balance.
atoms.effect: No frequency, hours or manner reasonably expected to abuse or harass.
judgment_terms: reasonably be expected to abuse or harass
atoms.quote: Communicate with the debtor or any member of his family or household with such frequency or at such unusual hours or in such a manner as can reasonably be expected to abuse or harass the debtor

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Threatening action (suit, reporting, referral).
atoms.effect: May not threaten any action the creditor does not in fact take in its usual course of business.
atoms.quote: Threaten any action which the principal creditor in the usual course of his business does not in fact take

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Claiming a right against the former tenant (e.g., retaining a forfeited deposit, a charge barred by statute).
atoms.effect: May not claim, attempt or threaten to enforce a right with knowledge or reason to know it does not exist.
atoms.quote: Claim, or attempt or threaten to enforce a right with knowledge or reason to know that the right does not exist

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Written demands for the balance.
atoms.effect: May not use a communication simulating legal or judicial process or appearing to be authorized by government or an attorney when it is not.
atoms.quote: Use a communication which simulates in any manner legal or judicial process or which gives the appearance of being authorized, issued or approved by a government, governmental agency, or attorney at law when it is not

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: principal creditor or its agent (landlord, manager, collector)
atoms.condition: Choosing a channel to collect.
atoms.effect: May not use a social media platform as a means to collect a consumer claim.
atoms.quote: Use a social media platform as a means to collect on a consumer claim from a debtor.

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Initial communication to the debtor about a consumer claim.
atoms.effect: Must clearly disclose that communications can be provided in an alternative accessible format (large print, braille, audio or other) chosen by the creditor, with a business phone number for requests.
atoms.quote: Each and every principal creditor or debt collector shall, in each initial communication, clearly and conspicuously disclose to the debtor that each communication can be provided in an alternative, reasonably accommodatable, format.

atoms.instrument: NY General Business Law art. 29-H
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Violation of GBL 601.
atoms.effect: Misdemeanor, each violation separate; AG or a district attorney may sue to restrain violations. (No private damages action stated for 601 in art. 29-H.)
atoms.quote: any person who violates the terms of section six hundred one of this article is guilty of a misdemeanor, and each such violation shall be deemed a separate offense.

atoms.instrument: NY CPLR
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Landlord sues a former tenant on the lease (rent, damage, other lease charges).
atoms.effect: Must be commenced within six years, unless 214-i (consumer credit) or another listed exception applies. A plaintiff that resided outside New York when the claim accrued (an owner entity based elsewhere, a tenant who had moved out of state) must also sue within its home state's period, with that state's tolling (NY:CPLR-202-borrowing).
atoms.quote: an action upon a contractual obligation or liability, express or implied, except as provided in section two hundred thirteen-a or two hundred fourteen-i of this article or article 2 of the uniform commercial code or article 36-B of the general business law

construction.quote: An action based upon a cause of action accruing without the state cannot be commenced after the expiration of the time limited by the laws of either the state or the place without the state where the cause of action accrued, except that where the cause of action accrued in favor of a resident of the state the time limited by the laws of the state shall apply.

atoms.reasoning: CPLR 202 holds a non-resident plaintiff to the shorter of New York's period and the period where the claim accrued.

atoms.instrument: NY CPLR
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: The action arises from a 'consumer credit transaction' (credit extended to an individual primarily for personal, family or household purposes) with the debtor as defendant.
atoms.effect: Three-year limit; later payments or acknowledgments do not revive it. Rent, use and occupancy and damage owed under a residential lease do not arise from a consumer credit transaction, so this section does not apply to them; CPLR 213(2) (six years) does (NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit).
atoms.quote: An action arising out of a consumer credit transaction where a purchaser, borrower or debtor is a defendant must be commenced within three years

atoms.instrument: NY Abandoned Property Law
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Money held in escrow or otherwise to ensure performance of a duty (e.g., a security deposit or its refund) remains unclaimed by the person entitled for three years, and the duty it secured is no longer to be performed.
atoms.effect: It is deemed abandoned property and must be paid to the State Comptroller with reports in the form the Comptroller prescribes.
judgment_terms: held ... to ensure the performance of any duty or obligation
atoms.quote: any amount representing unclaimed money or securities and held in escrow or otherwise by any corporation (other than a public corporation), joint stock company, individual, association of two or more individuals, committee or business trust, to ensure the performance of any duty or obligation, shall be deemed abandoned property when:

atoms.instrument: NY Abandoned Property Law
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Intangible property not otherwise subject to an unclaimed-property rule has gone unclaimed for two years.
atoms.effect: Holder may ask the Comptroller in writing to accept it; on payment it is deemed abandoned and the holder is relieved of liability to the extent of ABP 1404.
atoms.quote: Any person or entity who holds any intangible personal property, including the proceeds of a sale of tangible property, which is not otherwise subject to the provisions of this chapter or any other law regarding the disposition of unclaimed property belonging to any other person, and which has remained unclaimed for a period of two years by the person or persons appearing to be entitled to receive such property, may request in writing

atoms.instrument: NY State Technology Law art. III (ESRA)
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: A statement, notice or signature in this chain is made electronically (e.g., itemized statement by email).
atoms.effect: An electronic record has the same force and effect as a non-electronic record, and an electronic signature the same validity as a handwritten one, unless law provides otherwise (exceptions in STT 307 do not reach lease settlement documents).
judgment_terms: whether a statute's delivery requirement is satisfied by electronic transmission
atoms.quote: An electronic record shall have the same force and effect as those records not produced by electronic means.

atoms.instrument: NY State Technology Law art. III (ESRA)
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: Documents on disposition at death or incompetence, negotiable instruments/title documents, and documents the electronic facilitator excepts.
atoms.effect: ESRA does not apply to them. None is a deposit statement or notice in this chain (an uncashed refund check is a negotiable instrument).
atoms.quote: To any negotiable instruments and other instruments of title wherein possession of the instrument is deemed to confer title

atoms.instrument: 9 NYCRR (DHCR Tenant Protection Regulations under ETPA, outside NYC)
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: owner of an ETPA unit outside NYC
atoms.condition: Housing accommodation subject to ETPA outside NYC.
atoms.effect: Deposit may not exceed one month's rent (with a pre-1983 grandfather and a 65+ tenant rule); it must be in an interest-bearing bank account; owner takes 1%/yr; at the tenant's option the interest balance is applied to rent, held in trust until repaid, or paid annually; owner must otherwise comply with GOL art. 7.
atoms.quote: at the tenant's option, the balance of the interest paid by the banking organization shall be applied for the rental of the housing accommodation, or held in trust until repaid, or annually paid to the tenant; and (d) the owner otherwise complies with the provisions of article 7 of the General Obligations Law.

atoms.instrument: 9 NYCRR (State Rent and Eviction Regulations, rent control outside NYC)
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.actor: owner of a rent-controlled unit outside NYC
atoms.condition: Housing accommodation under the Emergency Housing Rent Control Law outside NYC (excluded from GOL 7-108(1-a)).
atoms.effect: Deposit allowed only up to one month's rent (one week for sub-monthly periods) and must be in an interest-bearing bank account; 1%/yr admin; interest balance held in trust until repaid or applied to rent, or paid annually; landlord must comply with GOL 7-103.
atoms.quote: the balance of the interest paid by the banking organization shall be held in trust until repaid or applied for the rental of the housing accommodations, or annually paid to the tenant; and (4) so long as the landlord complies with the provisions of section 7-103 of the General Obligations Law.

atoms.instrument: 14 E. 4th St. Unit 509 LLC v Toporek, 203 AD3d 17 (1st Dept 2022)
atoms.condition: Landlord failed to give the 7-108(1-a)(d) written notice of the right to a pre-vacate inspection, but did give a timely (e) itemized statement.
atoms.effect: No forfeiture: forfeiture attaches only to failure to meet (e). The court did not reach other remedies for a (d) failure; on its text, 7-108(1-a)(g) makes the violator liable for actual damages.
atoms.quote: by the plain terms of the statute only the obligations in paragraph (e) are subject to a penalty of forfeiture if they are not complied with

atoms.instrument: 14 E. 4th St. Unit 509 LLC v Toporek, 203 AD3d 17 (1st Dept 2022)
atoms.condition: Landlord sues an early-vacating residential tenant for rent.
atoms.effect: Mitigation is not a tenant affirmative defense; landlord must show reasonable and customary re-letting actions (online listings, showings, concessions sufficed). The unit need not actually be re-rented for the duty to be met.
atoms.quote: the statute does not require that the unit actually be re-rented in order to fulfill its duty to mitigate

atoms.instrument: Case v 575 Classon Ave., LLC, 81 Misc 3d 144(A), 2024 NY Slip Op 50199(U) (App Term, 2d Dept, 2d, 11th & 13th Jud Dists 2024)
atoms.provision: construing L.2019 c.36 Part M s.29; GOL 7-108(1-a)(e), (g); RPL 232-c
atoms.condition: Pre-HSTPA lease expired; landlord accepted rent for months after 2019-07-14.
atoms.effect: Acceptance of rent created a renewal tenancy (RPL 232-c) entered after the effective date, so 7-108(1-a) applied. 'Actual damages' for a missed 14-day statement equal the retained deposit, and a willfulness finding needs record support. The court did not reach the effect of forfeiture on a damage counterclaim because the landlord proved no damage (resolved in NY:ADJ-forfeiture-claims-survive).
atoms.quote: Upon defendant's acceptance of plaintiff's rent for January through May 2020, the parties created a renewal tenancy (*see* Real Property Law § 232-c; *Miske v Selvaggi*, 175 AD3d 1526 [2019]) and, therefore, the new provisions set forth in the HSTPA applied to this tenancy

atoms.instrument: Masseroli v Gatfield, 84 Misc 3d 487 (Sup Ct, Westchester County 2024)
atoms.condition: Landlord missed the 14-day statement and forfeited the deposit.
atoms.effect: The landlord must return the deposit but may still bring a separate claim for property damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, carrying the burden of proof (adopted in NY:ADJ-forfeiture-claims-survive). The court also treated the landlord's unawareness of the 2019 change as defeating willfulness; that reasoning is rejected in NY:ADJ-willful-standard.
judgment_terms: damage beyond ordinary wear and tear
atoms.quote: even though defendant failed to comply with her obligations in General Obligations Law § 7-108 (1-a) (e), she is not completely precluded from maintaining a separate action against plaintiff for any alleged property damages.

atoms.instrument: Pickens v Lane, 2023 NY Slip Op 50384(U) (Civ Ct, NY County 2023)
atoms.condition: Tenant left no forwarding mailing address but the landlord had the tenant's email.
atoms.effect: A statement mailed within 14 days to the vacated apartment did not 'provide' it; an email after day 14 was late; forfeiture followed. Forfeiture is of the right to retain the deposit, not of all claims: the landlord's counterclaim for rent before re-letting was allowed and netted.
atoms.quote: The forfeiture triggered upon by the landlord's noncompliance is the right to retain the security deposit; it is not a forfeiture of all claims against the tenant.

atoms.instrument: Mihalow v Rane, 2025 NY Slip Op 51234(U) (Sup Ct, NY County 2025)
atoms.condition: Landlord applies the deposit to unpaid rent.
atoms.effect: An itemized 14-day statement is still required; retention for rent arrears without one led to forfeiture.
atoms.quote: As the first of these grounds offered in that list is "non-payment of rent," entirely undercuts plaintiffs' argument that they could apply the security deposit toward rent arrears without providing defendants with an itemized statement explaining their rationale for retaining the entire deposit.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law art. 7 title 1
atoms.provision: GOL 7-107 heading and (1) as they stood before L.2025 c.436
atoms.effective_to: 2025-11-15 for leases, rental agreements and renewals entered into on or after that date (L.2025 c.436 s.2); continues to govern stabilized/ETPA leases and renewals entered into before it
atoms.actor: landlord of a stabilized/ETPA unit; successor owner
atoms.condition: Rent-stabilized (NYC RSL) or ETPA unit whose operative lease or renewal was entered into before 2025-11-15.
atoms.effect: Former 7-107 was titled and limited to the liability of a grantee or assignee for deposits on conveyance. Its only operative rules were successor liability (NY:GOL-7-107-pre2025(2)(a)), the receiver limit ((2)(b)) and the waiver bar ((3)). It set no deposit cap, no refund or itemization duty, no deadline and no forfeiture. Because 7-108(1) excludes every unit referred to in 7-107 (NY:GOL-7-108(1)), no state statute sets a return deadline, an itemized statement or a forfeiture for such a tenancy. What does govern it: 7-103 (trust, bank notice, interest), the common-law return rule (NY:COMMONLAW-deposit-return), the 7-103 commingling forfeiture (NY:CASE-Paterno-commingling-forfeiture), and the unit's rent regulation (NYC:RSC-2525.4 in NYC; NY:9NYCRR-2505.4 for ETPA outside NYC).
atoms.quote: § 7-107. [Liability of a grantee or assignee for deposits] Deposits made by tenants [upon conveyance] of rent stabilized dwelling units.

atoms.instrument: L.2025 c.436 (A6423-A/S952-B) Assembly sponsor memorandum
atoms.condition: Reading 7-107 and 7-108 as they stood 2019-07-14 to 2025-11-14 for a rent-stabilized unit.
atoms.effect: The sponsors state that the 2019 HSTPA deposit protections (14-day return, itemized statement, pre-vacate inspection) did not reach rent-stabilized units, because they were placed in 7-108, which excludes those units. The original S952 memo describes the fix as removing the exclusion of stabilized units. This confirms the plain reading of 7-108(1) and closes the question whether pre-2025 7-108(1-a) reached stabilized units: it did not.
atoms.quote: However, these protections do not extend to the hundreds of thousands of units that are rent stabilized, since the HSTPA included these protections in a Section of the General Obligations Law (7-108) that explicitly excludes rent stabilized dwelling units.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law art. 7 title 1
atoms.provision: GOL 7-108(1) as it stood before L.2019 c.36 Part M s.25
atoms.effective_to: 2019-07-14 for leases, rental agreements and renewals entered into on or after that date (Part M s.29); continues for leases entered into before it and not renewed since
atoms.condition: A lease entered into before 2019-07-14 with no renewal, renewal by rent acceptance (NY:RPL-232-c) or month-to-month continuation on or after that date.
atoms.effect: 7-108 applies only to dwelling units with written leases in premises of six or more units and to units under NYC or state rent control, and never to 7-107 (stabilized/ETPA) units. For such a lease 7-108 holds only successor liability (7-108(2)) and the waiver bar; 7-108(1-a) (cap, 14-day statement, forfeiture) does not apply. The deposit is then governed by 7-103 and the common-law return rule (NY:COMMONLAW-deposit-return).
atoms.quote: premises [containing six or more dwelling units and to all dwelling units subject to the city rent and rehabilitation law or the emergency housing rent control law], unless such dwelling unit is specifically referred to in section 7-107 of this [chapter] title.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Gable v Cahill, 69 Misc 3d 128(A) (App Term 2d Dept 2020), following earlier App Term decisions
atoms.effective_from: 2020-10-02 (decision; states the rule applied before HSTPA)
atoms.condition: A deposit held under 7-103 where no statutory return regime applies: rent-stabilized/ETPA leases entered before 2025-11-15; non-stabilized leases entered before 2019-07-14 and not renewed; rent-controlled units (excluded from 7-108(1-a)); other units excluded from 7-108(1-a).
atoms.effect: The deposit stays the tenant's property and must be returned at the conclusion of the tenancy unless the landlord proves damage beyond ordinary wear and tear (or another lawful application such as unpaid rent: NY:CASE-Gelbart-rent-offset). The landlord bears the burden of proving the damage and the reasonable value of the repairs. No fixed day count, no required itemized statement, no statutory forfeiture and no statutory punitive damages. Where 7-108(1-a) or amended 7-107 does apply, their 14-day rule and forfeiture are added on top.
judgment_terms: conclusion of the tenancy (no statutory day count)
damage beyond ordinary wear and tear
atoms.quote: must be returned at the conclusion of the tenancy, absent proof, for example, that the tenant caused damage beyond that attributable to ordinary wear and tear

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Gelbart v Spota, 2023 NY Slip Op 51404(U) (App Term 2d Dept 2023)
atoms.condition: A tenant sues to recover a deposit and the landlord proves unpaid rent.
atoms.effect: In the tenant's suit to recover the deposit, the landlord may offset proven unpaid rent against the amount owed. Where 7-108(1-a)(e) or amended 7-107(6) applies and no timely itemized statement was given, the deposit itself cannot be kept for the rent (NY:CASE-Mihalow-rent-arrears); the rent claim survives and is set off against the judgment or pursued by counterclaim (NY:ADJ-forfeiture-claims-survive).
atoms.quote: A landlord is also generally entitled to offset unpaid rent in an action commenced by a tenant to recover a security deposit

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.condition: The landlord did not give the tenant the 7-103(2) written notice of the bank holding the deposit.
atoms.effect: That failure permits an inference that the landlord commingled the deposit with its own money in violation of 7-103; the landlord must rebut it.
atoms.quote: Their showing that Paterno failed to give them written notice of the banking institution that held the deposit, in violation of General Obligations Law § 7-103, permitted an inference that Paterno violated General Obligations Law § 7-103 by commingling security deposit moneys with his own personal funds

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Paterno v Carroll, 75 AD3d 625 (2d Dept 2010); Gihon, LLC v 501 Second St., LLC, 103 AD3d 840 (2d Dept 2013)
atoms.condition: The landlord commingled the deposit with its own funds (proved, or inferred and not rebutted: NY:CASE-Paterno-bank-notice-inference). Applies to every 7-103 deposit, including stabilized, rent-controlled and pre-2019 tenancies that have no statutory 14-day forfeiture.
atoms.effect: The landlord forfeits the right to use the deposit for any purpose, and the tenant is entitled to its immediate return even if the tenant breached the lease. The landlord's separate claim for rent survives (NY:CASE-Paterno-rent-survives).
atoms.quote: As a result of such commingling, Paterno forfeited his right to avail himself of the deposit for any purpose, and the Carrolls have an immediate right to return of the funds notwithstanding that they may have breached the lease

construction.quote: it has been uniformly held that a commingling constitutes a conversion and entitles the tenant to the immediate recovery of his deposit or advances.

atoms.reasoning: The First Department holds the same (LeRoy v Sayers): commingling is a conversion entitling the tenant to immediate recovery, so the rule binds in all four departments' courts sitting in the city.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.condition: The landlord has forfeited the deposit for a 7-103 violation.
atoms.effect: The forfeiture does not relieve the tenant of the obligation to pay rent; the landlord may still pursue rent owed under the lease as a separate claim. The same rule governs the 7-108(1-a)(e) and 7-107(6) forfeitures (NY:ADJ-forfeiture-claims-survive).
atoms.quote: Paterno's violation of General Obligations Law § 7-103 did not relieve them of their obligation to pay rent

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Gihon, LLC v 501 Second St., LLC, 103 AD3d 840 (2d Dept 2013)
atoms.condition: Deciding whether 7-103(2-a) (interest-bearing account) applies.
atoms.effect: The test is the building: if it contains six or more family dwelling units, 7-103(2-a) applies, whatever the particular lease and even in a mixed commercial/residential building. Several buildings are not combined (NY:ADJ-7103-2a-building-count).
atoms.quote: The statute makes no exception for a mixed commercial/residential building, such as the subject property. The applicability of the statute is expressly conditioned on the nature of the building, and not on the nature of any particular lease referable to units within the building.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Karole v 340 W. End Ave., LLC, 74 Misc 3d 1233(A) (Civ Ct NY County 2022)
atoms.condition: Rent-stabilized tenant on a renewal lease entered before 2025-11-15 (vacated 2020) sues for the deposit.
atoms.effect: The court applied 7-108(1-a)(e) forfeiture and (g) double punitive damages to a stabilized unit, reasoning that RSC 2525.4 makes stabilized deposits subject to GOL art. 7. It did not address 7-108(1)'s exclusion of 7-107 units. Considered and rejected: see NY:ADJ-RS-pre2025-7108-inapplicable. Its willfulness reasoning is separate (NY:CASE-Karole-willful).
atoms.quote: As claimant correctly pointed out, Section 2525.4 of the Rent Stabilization Code provides that a security deposit paid by a tenant of a rent stabilized housing accommodation is subject to the provisions of article 7 of the General Obligations Law.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.condition: Tenant vacated on a known day; landlord sends the itemized statement later than 14 days after.
atoms.effect: Appellate Division applies the 14-day count with the vacating day excluded (vacated July 24 -> due August 7), consistent with GCN 20. A statement six days late fails 7-108(1-a)(e), so the landlord cannot win dismissal of the tenant's forfeiture claim.
atoms.quote: the Abruzzos had until August 7, 2020, to provide the plaintiff with an itemized statement

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.condition: The date the tenant vacated is disputed, e.g. the tenant left belongings, and the lease says the tenant has not moved out until its property is out.
atoms.effect: When the tenant 'vacated' for the 14-day clock is a question of fact, and a lease term defining move-out by removal of the tenant's property is not displaced by 7-108(1-a)(e). The clock anchor is therefore a judgment, informed by the lease.
judgment_terms: vacated (possession surrendered, including removal of belongings where the lease so provides)
atoms.quote: Thus, issues of fact exist as to whether plaintiff legally vacated more than 14 days before defendant's October 1, 2019 email providing the statement accounting for the withholding of the security deposit.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: 14 E. 4th St. Unit 509 LLC v Toporek, 203 AD3d 17 (1st Dept 2022)
atoms.condition: Repairs are not yet done when the 14-day statement is due.
atoms.effect: A timely statement that itemizes each item to be repaired, replaced or cleaned with its estimated cost (there with photographs) was a compliant itemized statement, so no forfeiture. Whether the items were needed and what they cost is for trial, where the landlord bears the burden (7-108(1-a)(f)). NY has no statutory follow-up statement; a shortfall beyond the deposit is pursued as a separate claim.
atoms.quote: Here there is no dispute that landlord provided tenant with such an itemized statement in a timely manner. The parties' further disputes regarding whether the itemized repairs were required and the cost of rectifying them are issues to be resolved at trial.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Bogom-Shanon v Altman, 2025 NY Slip Op 25279 (Civ Ct NY County 2025), following Albert v Bryant (Mt Vernon City Ct 2022) and Asquith v Redevelop Albany (Albany City Ct 2019)
atoms.condition: Landlord explains the retention to the tenant orally (e.g. by phone) within 14 days.
atoms.effect: Not compliant: the 'itemized statement' must be written, by letter, email, text or other written means. An oral explanation alone leads to forfeiture. Adopted in NY:ADJ-provide-written-dispatch.
atoms.quote: impliedly requires a *written* statement, whether by letter, email, text, or any other written means

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Bogom-Shanon v Altman, 2025 NY Slip Op 25279 (Civ Ct NY County 2025)
atoms.condition: A lease entered before 2019-07-14 expired after that date and the tenancy continued month to month.
atoms.effect: The month-to-month tenancy is subject to 7-108(1-a) (same result as NY:CASE-Case-v-575Classon on rent acceptance).
atoms.quote: Accordingly, the Court finds that the month-to-month tenancy at issue in this proceeding was subject to the HSTPA, including the provisions regarding security deposits.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Bogom-Shanon v Altman, 2025 NY Slip Op 25279 (Civ Ct NY County 2025)
atoms.condition: Landlord violated 7-108(1-a) believing its conduct was lawful.
atoms.effect: A unilateral mistake of law is no defense to willfulness, and unreasonable delay can itself show willfulness. Adopted in NY:ADJ-willful-standard, which rejects Masseroli's contrary treatment of an unaware landlord.
atoms.quote: a unilateral mistake of law, particularly where defendant is an attorney admitted in this state, is not a defense to liability

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Prando v Kelly, 73 Misc 3d 144(A) (App Term 2d Dept 2021)
atoms.condition: Deciding whether a landlord 'willfully' violated 7-108(1-a) (and, by identical text, amended 7-107(8)).
atoms.effect: Willfulness is a question of fact in which credibility is a factor. A late return the trial court found 'innocent' (the landlord did not know the tenant's new address) still meant forfeiture, but no punitive damages. The full standard is NY:ADJ-willful-standard.
atoms.quote: Willfulness is a factual determination with credibility being one of the factors

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Karole v 340 W. End Ave., LLC, 74 Misc 3d 1233(A) (Civ Ct NY County 2022)
atoms.condition: A management company handles the deposit return and misses the 14-day statement.
atoms.effect: A management company is held to know the deposit law, and its knowledge is imputed to the owner. Sending no statement and giving a pretextual reason supported a willfulness finding and double punitive damages. Adopted in NY:ADJ-willful-standard.
atoms.quote: The court finds that, as a management company, Kaye Equities, knew or should have known of General Obligations Law § 7-108, the law governing the return of security deposits.

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Levine v Xu-Kehrli, 2026 NY Slip Op 50528(U) (App Term 1st Dept 2026)
atoms.condition: Landlord missed the 14-day statement and also counterclaims for property damage.
atoms.effect: The Appellate Term affirmed both a full return of the deposit (forfeiture under 7-108(1-a)(e)) and a judgment deciding the landlord's damage counterclaim on its merits. The forfeiture did not bar the counterclaim; it succeeded or failed on proof. Adopted in NY:ADJ-forfeiture-claims-survive.
atoms.quote: in awarding plaintiff a return of her security deposit in the main action and in limiting defendant's recovery on her property damage counterclaim

atoms.instrument: NY interpretive authority (case law)
atoms.provision: Lefferts Ave. Ventures LLC v Keennlyside, 88 Misc 3d 1207(A) (Civ Ct Kings County 2026)
atoms.condition: Landlord sues a former tenant for rent arrears under a lease; tenant pleads the 3-year CPLR 214-i limit.
atoms.effect: Rent arrears are not a 'consumer credit transaction' under CPLR 105(f), so the six-year CPLR 213(2) limit applies. The court declined to follow Kings & Queens Holdings v Ahmad (Civ Ct Richmond County 2017). Adopted in NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law art. 7 title 1 (adjudication)
atoms.condition: A tenant seeks punitive damages of up to twice the deposit because the landlord 'willfully' violated 7-108(1-a) or amended 7-107.
atoms.effect: Willfulness is a finding of fact on the whole record, in which credibility is a factor, and the record must support it (Prando; Case v 575 Classon). It has two parts. The failure: it must be knowing, intentional or deliberate; negligence and inadvertence are not willful. Knowledge of the law: an experienced landlord, or its managing agent, is charged with knowing the deposit law, and the agent's knowledge is imputed to the owner, so a deliberate choice to keep the deposit without a timely written statement is willful whatever the landlord's reading of the law. A miss caused by an inadvertent error despite a working process (a misdated send, a failed delivery, a channel the tenant supplied that did not reach the manager's records) is not willful, even for a manager. Factors pointing to willfulness: no written statement at all; a pretextual reason for keeping the deposit; keeping it after a demand that cites the statute; long or unexplained delay; prior violations. Punitive damages are discretionary, 'up to' twice the deposit. An experienced landlord or managing agent is charged with knowing that the 14-day rule has no exception for a missing address, so its deliberate decision to hold the statement pending an address satisfies the knowledge element and is evidence of willfulness; whether the violation is willful, and the amount up to twice the deposit, is found on the whole record (Prando affirmed a finding that such a wait was innocent). Forfeiture follows the missed deadline regardless of intent.

The New York County Civil Court applied that meaning to 7-108 in Karole and Bogom-Shanon. The Appellate Terms leave the finding to the trial court on credibility and require record support (Prando; Case). Masseroli, a Westchester Supreme Court decision, treated a licensed broker's unawareness of the 2019 change as enough to defeat willfulness. That conflicts with the Appellate Division's should-have-known test, and a trial court does not displace it, so Masseroli's reasoning is rejected. Its result still fits the standard for an individual owner who is not experienced with the law and sent a late written statement. Karole states both parts: willful conduct is more than inadvertence and is done knowingly, intentionally or deliberately, and a professional is charged with knowing the law. atoms.condition: Choosing where to send the 14-day statement and refund. Branch (a): the tenant gave a forwarding address, or the landlord has the tenant's email or phone number. Branch (b): the landlord has no forwarding address and no email or phone number.
atoms.effect: (a) The landlord sends the statement to the forwarding address or by email to a known email address or by text message to a known phone number, and the refund to the forwarding address or by a payment directed to the tenant: an electronic payment to an account or payment address the landlord holds for the tenant, or, if it holds none, a check mailed to the last known postal address (the vacated unit), with the statement saying where and how the refund was sent. It does not hold the refund for an address. Mailing to the vacated unit when the landlord knows another channel is not providing the statement, and forfeiture follows. (b) The landlord sends the statement and refund within the 14 days to the tenant's last known address, the vacated unit. The deadline has no exception for a missing address: holding the statement and refund until the tenant supplies an address forfeits the right to retain, whether or not the wait is found willful (NY:ADJ-willful-standard). atoms.effect: The itemized statement goes to each co-tenant at the address or electronic channel the landlord has for that co-tenant. (a) The refund is a joint obligation: pay it by one payment to all co-tenants jointly or as all of them direct in writing; payment of the whole to one of them also discharges the landlord, and the co-tenants settle between themselves. (b) Each co-tenant owns the part he paid. Lawful deductions for the joint lease obligations come out of the whole deposit, and the remainder is paid to each co-tenant in proportion to what he paid, unless all of them direct otherwise in writing. Paying the whole remainder to one co-tenant does not discharge the landlord as to another co-tenant's part. An occupant who is not a party to the lease is not a payee (NY:RPL-235-f).

Where the landlord's records show that each co-tenant paid an identified part, 7-103(1) itself assigns each part to the person who paid it; that is a word of severance, which Lasky holds displaces the joint presumption. atoms.condition: The tenant has moved out voluntarily and left personal property in the unit or building. The property has not been abandoned (NY:COMMONLAW-belongings-abandonment).
atoms.effect: The property remains the tenant's. The landlord may not hold it until rent or charges are paid. It must let the owner retrieve it on request, and refusing access or disposing of the property is conversion, for which the landlord is liable for its value. The landlord owes no bailee's duty of care unless it agreed to keep the property. It may charge the reasonable cost of moving and storing the belongings against the deposit (NY:GOL-7-108(1-a)(b)-refundable; NY:GOL-7-107(3)-refundable) or claim it separately. Belongings left behind can also push back the date the tenant 'vacated' (NY:CASE-Urban-vacatur).

atoms.reasoning: No statute governs belongings left after a voluntary move-out, so the common law of conversion governs. The First Department treats a landlord's unreasonable refusal of access to a former tenant's property as conversion, and it dismissed a bailment claim because the landlord never agreed to keep the property (8902 Corp.). The Fourth Department holds that disposal is authorized only if the property was abandoned (Cretaro). Facey (Kings County Civil Court) described the landlord as a bailee; the First Department's rule that there is no bailment without an agreement governs instead. Facey's holding that a landlord may not hold property for rent stands. The statute separately lets moving and storage costs be retained from the deposit.

atoms.instrument: NY common law (abandonment of personal property)
atoms.provision: Disposal of belongings after a voluntary move-out
atoms.condition: The landlord wants to discard, donate or sell belongings a former tenant left behind.
atoms.effect: The landlord may dispose of the property only once it is abandoned, and then it is not liable for conversion. Abandonment is the owner's intentional relinquishment of all claim to the property. It is not presumed and must be shown by direct proof or by facts that leave no other inference. Evidence of abandonment: the tenant says so; the tenant surrendered the keys and removed everything else; the landlord gave written notice to the tenant's last known address and channels with a stated period to retrieve, tried to reach the tenant, and got no response for a substantial time (about six weeks sufficed in Henryka). Evidence against abandonment: the tenant removes part of the property, asks for more time, or asks for access. A landlord that disposes of property that was not abandoned is liable for its value.
atoms.quote: The abandonment of property is the relinquishing of all title, possession or claim to or of it—a virtual intentional throwing away of it. It is not presumed.

construction.quote: Proof supporting it must be direct or affirmative or reasonably beget the exclusive inference of the throwing away

atoms.reasoning: The Court of Appeals definition of abandonment (Foulke, 1920), applied by the Fourth Department in Cretaro, is the test. The Appellate Term, Second Department, which binds the Kings, Queens and Richmond County Civil Courts, applied it to a former tenant's belongings: waiting about six weeks and trying to reach the tenant made it reasonable to treat them as abandoned (Henryka). Cretaro shows the other side: partial removal and requests for more time defeat abandonment even after a 30-day notice. Some trial courts borrowed the UCC 7-206 warehouse-sale procedure after 30 days (Wilson v CRL Mgt., cited in Facey). No appellate court adopted it, and it does not displace the abandonment test. A landlord that follows those steps still has to meet the abandonment test.
