atoms.condition: A landlord or its managing agent collects, or sues for, a former residential tenant's unpaid rent, use and occupancy, or damage owed under the lease.
atoms.effect: The balance is not a 'consumer claim' under GBL 600(1) and does not arise from a 'consumer credit transaction' under CPLR 105(f), because it comes from breach of the lease, not from credit offered or extended. So GBL 601, 601-b and 602 do not govern the landlord's or its agent's collection of it, and the three-year CPLR 214-i period does not apply. Suit is timely within six years (CPLR 213(2)). Federal and city collection rules apply on their own terms (US:FDCPA-conduct; NYC layer). From the 90th day after S9760/A10182-A becomes law, suits on a lease balance against a natural person have a three-year limit (NY:CPLR-214-i-consumer-debt-S9760).
atoms.quote: credit is extended to an individual

construction.quote: arises out of a transaction wherein credit has been offered or extended to a natural person
does not derive from an extension of credit
This Court is not aware of any controlling authority extending the definition of consumer credit transactions under CPLR 105 (f) to unpaid rent arrears.
Further, when the plaintiff let the defendant vacate the apartment without paying the rent an extension of credit occurred.
We have long held that the statutory text is the clearest indicator of legislative intent

atoms.reasoning: Both definitions turn on a transaction in which credit is offered or extended. A lease exchanges possession for rent. Unpaid rent is a breach of that exchange, not credit: the Second Circuit said so in Romea while holding that back rent is still a 'debt' under the broader FDCPA definition, which has no credit element. Lefferts (Kings County Civil Court, 2026) applies that reading and declines to follow Kings & Queens Holdings (Richmond County Civil Court, 2017). Kings & Queens rested on a misreading of Romea and on the view that letting a tenant leave without paying extends credit, which would turn every unpaid bill into credit. No appellate court has decided the point. The text of both statutes, Romea's analysis and the later, fuller trial decision agree, so Lefferts prevails. Kings & Queens is rejected.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law 7-103(2-a) (adjudication)
atoms.provision: GOL 7-103(2-a) ('property containing six or more family dwelling units')
atoms.condition: Deciding whether a deposit must be held in an interest-bearing account under 7-103(2-a), where the rented unit is in a building with fewer than six family dwelling units and the owner also owns other buildings, on the same lot, in a complex or elsewhere.
atoms.effect: Count the family dwelling units in the building that contains the rented unit. Dwelling units in the owner's other buildings are not added, even on the same lot or in one complex. Commercial units are not counted, but a mixed-use building with six or more dwelling units is covered. If the building has fewer than six dwelling units, 7-103(2-a) does not require an interest-bearing account. The 7-103(1) trust and the 7-103(2) bank notice and interest rules still apply if the landlord banks the deposit.
atoms.quote: The applicability of the statute is expressly conditioned on the nature of the building, and not on the nature of any particular lease referable to units within the building.

construction.quote: The applicability of the statute is expressly conditioned on the nature of the building, and not on the nature of any particular lease referable to units within the building.
This bill, except for the limitation in its application to buildings with six or more apartments
the building in which the apartment is located contains six or more family dwelling units
State law requires that money paid as security to rent an apartment in a building that contains six or more family dwelling units be deposited in an interest-bearing account in New York.
The courts may not enlarge the wording of a statute even in favor of what may be deemed an equitable construction.

atoms.reasoning: The Second Department reads 'property containing six or more family dwelling units' as a test of the building (Gihon). The Governor's 1970 approval memorandum, quoted in State v Parker, describes the limit as 'buildings with six or more apartments'. The Appellate Term (Holmes) and the Attorney General's 2014 opinion state the same building test. The Attorney General's opinion also refers to 'large residential landlords' of six or more units. That describes the purpose, which was to spare small landlords the clerical cost; it does not add a rule that combines separate buildings. Combining an owner's buildings would enlarge the words, which courts may not do (Lefkowitz v Parker, First Department). The building test prevails.

atoms.instrument: NY common law of monthly tenancies; RPL 232-a, 232-b (adjudication)
atoms.provision: Tenant's termination of a monthly or month-to-month tenancy in New York City
atoms.condition: A residential monthly or month-to-month tenancy in New York City, including one created by the landlord accepting rent after a lease expired (RPL 232-c). The tenant ends it, and no lease term or other agreement requires the tenant to give notice.
atoms.effect: The tenant may end the tenancy by surrendering possession at the end of any monthly term without prior notice. Rent is owed for each monthly term the tenant has begun, including the one in which it surrenders, and for no later month. RPL 232-a governs only the landlord's notice. RPL 232-b's one-month tenant notice applies only outside New York City.
atoms.quote: so a monthly tenant or tenant from month to month may surrender at the end of any month without notice.

construction.quote: imposes by implication a reciprocal obligation on such tenants to give thirty days’ prior notice to the landlord of their intention to vacate
Motion for leave to appeal to the Court of Appeals or for a reargument denied
held that there was no obligation on the part of a month-to-month tenant to give thirty days’ notice to the landlord in order to terminate his tenancy
Hence where the duration of the term is fixed, there is no rule nor any reason for a rule, requiring any notice to quit to be given.

month to month of any lands or buildings located outside of
the city of New York may be terminated by the tenant
an irrefutable inference must be drawn that what is omitted or not included was intended to be omitted or excluded
no statutory obligation to give defendants notice of an intent to vacate

atoms.reasoning: The Appellate Term, First Department, held in T.I.B. Corp. v Repetto that a New York City month-to-month tenant may surrender at the end of any month without notice. It rejected the argument that the landlord's notice statute (now RPL 232-a) implies a matching duty on the tenant. The Appellate Division affirmed and denied leave to appeal (261 App Div 813, 943), and later courts followed the rule (Andriola). It rests on the Court of Appeals rule that a tenancy for a fixed term needs no notice to quit (Adams v City of Cohoes). The Legislature later imposed a tenant's one-month notice only 'outside of the city of New York' (RPL 232-b) and left 232-a as a limit on landlords, including when it rewrote both sections in 2019. Where a law expressly covers some places, the places it leaves out were left out on purpose (Colon, Court of Appeals, McKinney's Statutes 240). No later decision imposes a notice duty on the NYC tenant. The Appellate Term, Second Department, holds the same (Srinivasan v Silvi), so the rule is the same in all five counties.

atoms.instrument: NY common law of contracts and monthly tenancies (adjudication)
atoms.provision: Tenant's notice under an agreement, NYC monthly or month-to-month tenancy
atoms.condition: A residential monthly or month-to-month tenancy in New York City in which a lease term or other agreement, express or implied, requires the tenant to give notice before ending the tenancy, and the tenant leaves on shorter notice.
atoms.effect: The agreement governs. The tenant owes rent through the end of the agreed notice period, measured to the end of a monthly term (GCN 30 for month counts; GCN 25 for contract periods ending on a weekend or holiday). That claim is subject to the landlord's duty to mitigate (NY:RPL-227-e), and the landlord carries the burden of proving it.
atoms.quote: Cases in which there was a monthly rental and an agreement for notice

construction.quote: unless an agreement either express or implied is made providing otherwise
Whether an agreement for a term different than month to month may be implied is a question of fact.

atoms.reasoning: T.I.B. Corp. distinguished cases where the monthly letting came with an agreement for notice; the no-notice rule applies only without one. RPL 232-c lets the parties' express or implied agreement set the terms of a tenancy created by accepting rent after the lease expired, and whether such an agreement exists is a question of fact (Palumbo). Rent claimed after an early departure is damages for leaving in breach of the agreement, so RPL 227-e's mitigation duty and burden apply.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law 7-108(1-a)(b), 7-107(3) read with RPAPL 702 (adjudication)
atoms.condition: The unit is under 7-108(1-a) or amended 7-107. At move-out the ledger carries late fees, returned-check fees or other fees or charges that are not unpaid rent, damage caused by the tenant beyond normal wear and tear, utility charges payable directly to the landlord under the lease, or moving and storage of the tenant's belongings.
atoms.effect: Those fees may not be retained from the deposit, even if the lease calls them 'additional rent'. The amount must be refunded within the 14 days. A fee that is lawful in itself (for example a late fee within RPL 238-a(2), or a returned-check charge within RPL 238-a(2-a)) may be pursued separately. Legal fees need a court order (NY:RPL-234-a).
atoms.quote: The entire amount of the deposit or advance shall be refundable to the tenant upon the tenant's vacating of the premises except for an amount lawfully retained for the reasonable and itemized costs due to non-payment of rent

construction.quote: The entire amount of the deposit or advance shall be refundable to the tenant upon the tenant's vacating of the premises except for an amount lawfully retained for the reasonable and itemized costs due to non-payment of rent
an irrefutable inference must be drawn that what is omitted or not included was intended to be omitted or excluded
a statute must be construed as a whole and . . . its various sections must be considered together and with reference to each other

the term "rent" shall
mean the monthly or weekly amount charged in consideration for the use
and occupation of a dwelling pursuant to a written or oral rental
agreement.

No fees, charges or penalties other than rent may be sought
in a summary proceeding pursuant to this article, notwithstanding any
language to the contrary in any lease or rental agreement.
Any agreement by a lessee or tenant of a dwelling waiving or modifying his rights as set forth in this section shall be absolutely void.
Plaintiff lawfully retained the security deposit for "the non-payment of rent" and "the non-payment of utility charges"

atoms.reasoning: The statute makes the entire deposit refundable except for four named costs. Under the Court of Appeals' reading of McKinney's Statutes 240 (Colon), what a list leaves out is excluded. A late fee is a charge for paying late, not unpaid rent, and it is not a 'cost due to non-payment of rent': that cost is the rent itself. The same 2019 act (L.2019 c.36 Part M) defined 'rent' in RPAPL 702 as the monthly amount for use and occupation and barred fees 'notwithstanding any language to the contrary in any lease'. Read together, as sections of one act must be (Colon), the Legislature drew the line between rent and fees in that act. A lease clause relabeling fees as rent cannot widen the categories, because any agreement modifying the tenant's 7-108 rights is void (7-108(3); 7-107(10) for stabilized units). The First Department approved retention by naming the statutory categories, rent and utility charges (Freeland).

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law 7-103(1) and common-law return rule (adjudication)
atoms.provision: GOL 7-103(1) (deposit as security for the contract)
atoms.condition: The deposit is governed by the common-law return rule, not by 7-108(1-a) or amended 7-107: a stabilized/ETPA lease or renewal entered before 2025-11-15, a non-stabilized lease entered before 2019-07-14 and not renewed, or a rent-controlled unit.
atoms.effect: The deposit secures performance of the lease. At the end of the tenancy it may be applied to sums lawfully due under the lease, including a late fee or returned-check charge that complies with RPL 238-a, as well as unpaid rent and proven damage. Any city-layer bar on the charge itself (NYC.json) still applies. The landlord bears the burden of proving each amount applied, and the balance must be returned (NY:COMMONLAW-deposit-return).
atoms.quote:
as security for performance of the contract
or agreement or to be applied to payments upon such contract or
agreement when due

construction.quote:
as security for performance of the contract
or agreement or to be applied to payments upon such contract or
agreement when due
A landlord is also generally entitled to offset unpaid rent in an action commenced by a tenant to recover a security deposit

atoms.reasoning: Where no statute lists what may be retained, 7-103(1) defines the deposit as security for performance of the contract, or money to be applied to payments due under it. A lawful late fee is a payment due under the lease. The Appellate Term allows the deposit to be applied to what the tenant owes under the lease (Gelbart: unpaid rent), and the common-law rule puts the burden of proof on the landlord. The 7-108(1-a) list does not reach these tenancies (NY:ADJ-RS-pre2025-7108-inapplicable; NY:GOL-7-108(1)-pre2019).

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.effective_from: in force at retrieval 2026-09-28; enactment date not read
atoms.condition: The landlord claims rent or use and occupancy from a former tenant for a period in which the premises or common areas were unfit for habitation or had conditions dangerous to life, health or safety that the tenant or persons under the tenant's control did not cause.
atoms.effect: Every residential lease carries the warranty of habitability. The tenant's damages for its breach offset the rent or use and occupancy owed for that period. A condition caused by the tenant's misconduct is not a breach. A waiver is void. For a rent-regulated unit, the damages are reduced by any DHCR rent reduction ordered for the same condition. No expert testimony is required to fix the amount.
judgment_terms: conditions dangerous, hazardous or detrimental to life, health or safety
atoms.quote:
In every written or oral lease
or rental agreement for residential  premises  the  landlord  or  lessor
shall  be  deemed to covenant and warrant that the premises so leased or
rented and all areas used in connection therewith in common  with  other
tenants  or  residents  are  fit  for  human habitation

atoms.instrument: NY CPLR art. 50
atoms.condition: A landlord recovers a sum from a former tenant for breach of the lease (unpaid rent, use and occupancy, damage or another lease charge).
atoms.effect: Interest is recovered on the sum as of right, computed from the earliest date each amount was due (or from a single reasonable intermediate date where amounts fell due at different times). The rate is NY:CPLR-5004(a)-consumer-2pct unless the lease sets one (NY:CASE-NML-contract-rate).
atoms.quote: Interest shall be recovered upon a sum awarded because of a breach of performance of a contract

atoms.effective_from: 2022-04-30 (120th day after L.2021 c.831 became law) for judgments entered on or after that date
atoms.instrument: NY CPLR art. 50, as amended by L.2021 c.831
atoms.condition: The statutory rate of interest applies to a claim against a former tenant (no lease rate governs: NY:CASE-NML-contract-rate), before or after judgment (CPLR 5001-5003).
atoms.effect: Branch (a): the defendant is a natural person (tenant or individual guarantor). A residential lease balance is a 'consumer debt' under 5004(b), so the rate is 2% a year for judgments entered on or after 2022-04-30; on the unpaid part of a judgment entered earlier, post-judgment interest runs at 2% from that date. Branch (b): the tenant is a company or other entity: 9% a year. The ruling that a lease balance is not consumer credit (NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit) does not change this, because 5004(b) defines consumer debt by purpose and includes consumer credit only as one example.
atoms.quote: provided the annual rate of interest to be paid in an action arising out of a consumer debt where a natural person is a defendant shall be two per centum per annum

construction.quote: "consumer debt" means any obligation or alleged obligation of any natural person to pay money arising out of a transaction in which the money, property, insurance or services which are the subject of the transaction are primarily for personal, family or household purposes
including, but not limited to, a consumer credit transaction
this court determines residential rent arrears/unpaid rent is deemed a consumer debt pursuant to CPLR 5004
This act shall take effect on the one hundred twentieth day after

atoms.reasoning: 5004(b) defines consumer debt by the purpose of the transaction, and a residential lease is a transaction for personal, family or household purposes. The definition names consumer credit as one example and is not limited to it, so a balance that is not consumer credit under CPLR 105(f) is still a consumer debt here. Allen v Whidbee applies the 2% rate to residential rent arrears for that reason. L.2021 c.831 took effect on the 120th day after it became law, 2022-04-30.

atoms.instrument: NML Capital v Republic of Argentina, 17 NY3d 250 (2011) (Court of Appeals)
atoms.condition: The lease sets an interest rate that applies to amounts after they fall due (for example 'interest at X% on any sum not paid when due').
atoms.effect: The lease rate governs interest on those amounts until the claim is merged in a judgment; after judgment the statutory rate applies (NY:CPLR-5004(a)-consumer-2pct). Where the lease sets no rate for amounts after they fall due, the statutory rate applies from the start. Interest charged on late or unpaid rent is limited separately by NY:ADJ-lease-interest-on-rent. A rate the lease states without a period is a yearly rate (NY:GOL-5-1301-rate-per-annum).
atoms.quote: If the parties failed to include a provision in the contract addressing the interest rate that governs after principal is due or in the event of a breach, New York’s statutory rate will be applied as the default rate

construction.quote: any certain rate of interest is or shall be mentioned, and no period of time is stated for which such rate is to be calculated, interest shall be calculated at the rate mentioned, by the year, in the same manner as if the words “per annum” or “by the year” had been added to such rate.

atoms.reasoning: GOL 5-1301 reads a rate stated without a period as a yearly rate.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7 (adjudication)
atoms.condition: A residential lease charges interest on rent that is paid late or remains unpaid.
atoms.effect: That interest is a 'payment, fee, or charge for the late payment of rent'. It may not be demanded unless rent is more than five days late, and together with any late fee it may not exceed the lesser of $50 or 5% of the monthly rent (NY:RPL-238-a(2)); a lease term allowing more is void (NY:RPL-238-a(3)). Statutory interest a court awards on unpaid rent under CPLR 5001 and 5004 is not a charge the landlord demands and is not limited by 238-a.
atoms.quote: No landlord, lessor, sub-lessor or grantor may demand any payment, fee, or charge for the late payment of rent

construction.quote: No landlord, lessor, sub-lessor or grantor may demand any payment, fee, or charge for the late payment of rent unless the payment of rent has not been made within five days of the date it was due

atoms.reasoning: Interest on rent paid late is money charged because the rent was paid late, which is what 238-a(2) limits. The section reaches 'any' such payment, fee or charge the landlord demands, so a lease label does not take it outside the cap. A court's award of statutory interest is not a demand by the landlord.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law art. 5 title 9
atoms.condition: The lease says its term is deemed renewed for a further period unless the tenant gives notice of intent to quit.
atoms.effect: The renewal clause binds the tenant only if the landlord gave written notice, personally or by registered or certified mail, at least 15 and not more than 30 days before the tenant's notice deadline, calling attention to the clause. Without that notice the term ends on its stated date, the tenant owes no rent for the renewal period, and the settlement runs from the actual vacate date. With it, and no tenant notice, the renewal term binds, and rent after an early departure is limited by NY:RPL-227-e.
atoms.quote: shall be operative unless the lessor, at least fifteen days and not more than thirty days previous to the time specified for the furnishing of such notice to him, shall give to the tenant written notice, served personally or by registered or certified mail, calling the attention of the tenant to the existence of such provision in the lease

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 6-A (Good Cause Eviction Law)
atoms.condition: A housing accommodation in New York City.
atoms.effect: Article 6-A (Good Cause Eviction) applies in the city, subject to the exemptions in NY:RPL-214.
atoms.quote: Upon the effective date of this section, this article shall apply to the city of New York.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 6-A (Good Cause Eviction Law)
atoms.condition: Deciding whether the owner is a 'small landlord' exempt under RPL 214(1).
atoms.effect: A small landlord owns no more than ten units in the state. A natural-person owner counts every unit it owns or beneficially owns, directly or indirectly; with several natural-person owners, none may own more than ten; an entity is a small landlord only if each natural person with a direct or indirect interest in it or an affiliate owns no more than ten.
atoms.quote: The term "small landlord" as used in this article shall mean a landlord of no more than (i) ten units in the state

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 6-A (Good Cause Eviction Law)
atoms.condition: A market-rate housing accommodation in New York City.
atoms.effect: Article 6-A covers it unless one of the fifteen exemptions applies: (1) a small landlord (NY:RPL-211(3)-small-landlord); (2) an owner-occupied building of no more than ten units; (3) a unit sublet under RPL 226-b that the sublessor in good faith recovers for personal use; (4) housing solely incident to employment that has lawfully ended; (5) a unit regulated under other law; (6) a unit income-restricted by statute, regulation or regulatory agreement; (7) a condominium or cooperative unit, or one under an Attorney General offering plan; (8) a building whose certificate of occupancy issued on or after 2009-01-01, for thirty years; (9) a seasonal use unit; (10) hospitals, licensed senior and care facilities; (11) a manufactured home in a park; (12) hotel or transient class B use; (13) a school or college dormitory; (14) housing within a religious facility; (15) a unit whose monthly rent exceeds 245% of HUD fair market rent (NY:RPL-214(15)-high-rent).
atoms.quote: owner-occupied housing accommodation with no more then ten units

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 6-A (Good Cause Eviction Law)
atoms.condition: The unit is covered by article 6-A (NY:RPL-214) and the landlord wants the tenancy to end by not renewing the lease.
atoms.effect: The landlord may not remove the tenant by failure to renew, or otherwise, except on a court order that finds a good-cause ground listed in RPL 216. A 226-c non-renewal notice alone does not end a covered tenancy or start the settlement: the chain starts when the tenant actually leaves or a court orders removal. A tenant who stays after a non-renewal is not a holdover to be charged as one (NY:RPL-229, NY:RPL-220). An exempt unit ends as NY:RPL-226-c(1)(a) states.
atoms.quote: No landlord shall, by action to evict or to recover possession, by exclusion from possession, by failure to renew any lease, or otherwise, remove any tenant from housing accommodations covered by section two hundred fourteen of this article except for good cause as defined in section two hundred sixteen of this article.

construction.quote: except upon order of a court of competent jurisdiction entered in an appropriate judicial action or proceeding in which the petitioner or plaintiff has established one of the following grounds as good cause for removal or eviction

atoms.reasoning: 215 bars removal 'by failure to renew any lease, or otherwise' without good cause, and 216 requires a court order on a listed ground. A non-renewal notice is therefore not a lawful end of a covered tenancy by itself, so it does not create the departure from which the settlement runs.

atoms.instrument: NY CPLR art. 32 (Justia compilation; nysenate.gov returns 'not found' for this rule)
atoms.condition: A landlord or collector seeks a default judgment against a natural-person former tenant for nonpayment of the lease.
atoms.effect: At least 20 days before entry, mail a copy of the summons by first-class mail to the tenant's residence in an envelope marked 'personal and confidential' that does not show it is from an attorney or concerns a debt (if returned or the residence is unknown, to the place of employment), and file an affidavit of that mailing. This is in addition to the military-service affidavit (US:50USC3931(b)(1)). It does not apply in the small claims part of any court or in a summary proceeding to recover possession; it applies in the commercial claims part and in plenary actions.
atoms.quote: When a default judgment based upon nonappearance is sought against a natural person in an action based upon nonpayment of a contractual obligation an affidavit shall be submitted that additional notice has been given by or on behalf of the plaintiff at least twenty days before the entry of such judgment

construction.quote: This requirement shall not apply to cases in the small claims part of any court

atoms.reasoning: Subparagraph (iii) excludes the small claims part and summary proceedings from the mailing.

atoms.instrument: NYC Civil Court Act art. 18
atoms.condition: The owner that would sue a former tenant for a small balance is a corporation, partnership, association or LLC, or is an assignee of the claim.
atoms.effect: It may not bring the claim in the small claims part; an LLC is treated like a corporation or association for this purpose. It may use the commercial claims part only when NY:CCA-1801-A(a)-eligibility is met; otherwise it sues in the regular part of the Civil Court within its monetary limit, or in a court where the tenant can be sued.
atoms.quote: no partnership, or association and no assignee of any small claim shall institute an action or proceeding under this article

construction.quote: the action was properly commenced in the Commercial Claims Part of the Civil Court by plaintiff, a limited liability company that had its principal office in the State of New York

atoms.reasoning: CCA 1809(1) bars corporations, partnerships, associations and assignees from small claims; the Appellate Term, First Department, treats an LLC with a New York principal office as a proper commercial claims claimant, which places it on the corporate side of the line.

atoms.instrument: NYC Civil Court Act art. 18-A
atoms.condition: A commercial claim against a natural-person former tenant under a residential lease.
atoms.effect: The claim arises from a 'consumer transaction', so the consumer-transaction procedure in NY:CCA-1803-A(b) applies.
atoms.quote: The term "consumer transaction" means a transaction between a claimant and a natural person, wherein the money, property or service which is the subject of the transaction is primarily for personal, family or household purposes.

atoms.instrument: NYC Civil Court Act art. 18-A
atoms.condition: An entity owner eligible under NY:CCA-1801-A(a)-eligibility brings a commercial claim against a natural-person former tenant on a residential lease (NY:CCA-1801-A(b)).
atoms.effect: Before filing, it mails the OCA-form demand letter by ordinary first-class mail 10 to 180 days before commencing, stating the transaction date, the unpaid amount, the underlying document and an accounting of payments; at filing it certifies that mailing and that it has brought no more than five such actions that calendar month. Without a proper certificate the action does not proceed.
atoms.quote: the claimant has mailed by ordinary first class mail to the party complained against a demand letter, no less than ten days and no more than one hundred eighty days prior to the commencement of the claim

atoms.instrument: NY Multiple Dwelling Law
atoms.condition: Deciding whether a New York City building is a multiple dwelling.
atoms.effect: A multiple dwelling is a dwelling rented, or occupied, as the residence of three or more families living independently. The count is how the building is actually let or occupied, so a house certified for one or two families but let to three is a multiple dwelling (a de facto multiple dwelling).
atoms.quote: is occupied as the residence or home of three or more families living independently of each other.

atoms.instrument: NY Multiple Dwelling Law
atoms.condition: A multiple dwelling in New York City (NY:MDL-4(7)-multiple-dwelling).
atoms.effect: A certificate of occupancy is required before occupancy for a dwelling constructed as, or altered or converted into, a multiple dwelling after 1929-04-18, including a one- or two-family house later let to three or more families. No certificate is required for (a) a class B multiple dwelling existing on 1929-04-18 that did not need one before and has not been altered except in compliance, or (b) an old-law tenement, or a class A multiple dwelling erected after 1901-04-12 and occupied for the two years before 1909-01-01, not altered except in compliance, or altered only by combining two or more apartments into larger units so that the building's total legal number of families decreases without increasing its bulk. A temporary certificate of compliance or occupancy issued under MDL 301(4), while in force, satisfies the requirement for the part and use it covers. Evidence input: construction or conversion date and alteration history (Department of Buildings record), not the mere absence of a certificate. Consequence for rent: NY:MDL-302(1)(b).
atoms.quote: No multiple dwelling shall be occupied in whole or in part until the issuance of a certificate by the department

construction.quote: except that no such certificate shall be required in the case of:
Any old-law tenement, or any class A multiple dwelling erected after April twelfth, nineteen hundred one, which was occupied for two years immediately before January first, nineteen hundred nine

no dwelling constructed as or altered or converted into a multiple dwelling after April eighteenth, nineteen hundred twenty-nine, shall be occupied in whole or in part until the issuance of a certificate of compliance or
(1) two or more apartments are combined creating larger residential units, and
issue a temporary certificate of compliance or occupancy for a multiple dwelling or a section or a part thereof for a period of ninety days or less

atoms.reasoning: Subdivision 1 excepts the listed older buildings from the certificate requirement, and subdivision 2 applies the requirement to dwellings built as or converted into multiple dwellings after 1929-04-18. A building within an exception is lawfully occupied without a certificate. Subdivision 1(b) extends the exception to old-law tenements and qualifying class A buildings whose apartments were combined, reducing the family count without added bulk. Subdivision 4 authorizes temporary certificates; occupancy under one in force is occupancy under a certificate.

judgment_terms: tenant actually interfered with the owner's attempt to legalize
atoms.instrument: NY Multiple Dwelling Law
atoms.condition: The unit is in a multiple dwelling, including a de facto one, that was occupied during the period claimed in violation of MDL 301: it needed a certificate of occupancy for that residential use and had neither a permanent certificate nor a temporary one under MDL 301(4) in force (NY:MDL-301(1)). A building within the MDL 301(1)(a)-(b) exceptions is not occupied in violation.
atoms.effect: The owner recovers no rent and no use and occupancy for that period: not by suit, counterclaim or setoff, and not by keeping the deposit for it, so no rent for that period may be retained on the 14-day statement. A certificate obtained later does not revive rent for the unlawful period. Claims for damage and other non-rent charges are unaffected. The only exception: the tenant actually prevented the owner from legalizing the building.
atoms.quote: No rent shall be recovered by the owner of such premises for said period, and no action or special proceeding shall be maintained therefor

construction.quote: The command of Multiple Dwelling Law § 302 (1) (b) is, by its terms, absolute.

An owner of a de facto multiple dwelling who fails to obtain a proper certificate of occupancy or comply with the registration requirements of the Multiple Dwelling Law cannot recover for rent or money for use and occupancy
where the tenant actually interfered with the owner's
was precluded from charging respondents rent or other remuneration while the building lacked a certificate of occupancy for residential use
In the absence of compliance, the law's command is quite clear
shall continue to be the money of the person making such deposit or advance
occupied in whole or in part for human habitation in violation of section three hundred one

atoms.reasoning: The statute bars recovery of rent for the period of unlawful occupancy. Both Appellate Division departments apply it as written, to use and occupancy too, and the Court of Appeals reads it by its text. The deposit is the tenant's money held in trust, so keeping it for rent of that period is recovering that rent. The Chatsworth exception, stated in Caldwell, reaches only a tenant who actually interfered with legalization.

atoms.instrument: NY Multiple Dwelling Law
atoms.condition: The unit is in a New York City multiple dwelling and the owner has not filed the HPD registration the city requires (NYC:ADC-27-2097-registration).
atoms.effect: While unregistered, the owner recovers no rent, by suit, setoff or keeping the deposit for it. The bar is a suspension, not a forfeiture: once the owner registers, it recovers all rent that accrued while it was unregistered. Operator step: confirm current registration before the 14-day statement; if it is missing, file it before the statement goes out, so the deposit may be applied to rent. The city's stay and loss of possession for nonpayment (NYC:ADC-27-2107(b)-rent-stay) also apply to a multiple dwelling, and this bar controls; a one- or two-family house that must register faces only the city stay. Rent the tenant paid voluntarily while the owner was unregistered stays paid: the tenant cannot recover it, and it is not refunded or credited on the move-out account (payment under a judgment is not voluntary). Damage claims are not claims for rent.
atoms.quote: no rent shall be recovered by the owner of a multiple dwelling who fails to comply with such registration requirements until he complies with such requirements.

construction.quote: hold that, upon registering, an owner is entitled to recover the rents which accrued during the period of noncompliance

If a resident of an unregistered dwelling voluntarily pays rent or an installment of rent when he had a right to withhold the same under this subdivision, he shall not thereafter have any claim or cause of action to recover back the rent or installment of rent so paid.

atoms.reasoning: MDL 325(2) bars recovery 'until he complies'. The Appellate Term, Second Department (9 Montague Terrace), holds that on registering the owner recovers the rent that accrued while unregistered; the statute provides no abatement. No appellate decision holds otherwise.

atoms.instrument: NY Multiple Dwelling Law
atoms.condition: The unit is in a New York City multiple dwelling; HPD's records note a rent-impairing violation (a fire hazard or a serious threat to life, health or safety) in the unit or in a common part, with notice mailed to the registered owner, and the violation was not cleared within six months of that notice (or, where corrective work needs approved plans filed within three months, within six months of plan approval).
atoms.effect: For the period the violation stays uncorrected after the six months, the owner recovers no rent for that unit (for every unit, where the condition is in a common part or a part the owner controls), so none may be retained from the deposit for that period. The bar does not apply if the condition did not exist, was in fact corrected though the record was not cleared, was caused by the departing tenant or its household or guests or by another resident, or the tenant refused the owner entry to correct it. Rent the tenant paid voluntarily for the period cannot be recovered back by the tenant. In an owner's suit the tenant must plead the facts and deposit the rent claimed with the court clerk. Evidence inputs: HPD record, repair record, access refusals, cause of the condition.
atoms.quote: no rent shall be recovered by any owner for any premises in such multiple dwelling used by a resident thereof for human habitation in which the condition constituting such rent impairing violation exists

construction.quote: must also deposit with the clerk of the court in which the action or proceeding is pending at the time of filing of the resident's answer the amount of rent sought to be recovered
the condition which is the subject of the violation has in fact been corrected, though the note thereof in the department has not been removed or cancelled
the violation has been caused by the resident from whom rent is sought to be collected or by members of his family or by his guests
the resident proceeded against for rent has refused entry to the owner for the purpose of correcting the condition giving rise to the violation

If a resident voluntarily pays rent or an installment of rent when he would be privileged to withhold the same under subparagraph a, he shall not thereafter have any claim or cause of action to recover back the rent

atoms.reasoning: Subdivision 3 bars recovery of rent for the period; the plead-and-deposit condition applies to the tenant's defense in an owner's action and secures the rent for the owner if it prevails there. It creates no right to recover. Keeping the deposit for that period's rent is recovering it, so it is barred.

atoms.effective_from: the 90th day after S9760/A10182-A becomes law; passed Senate 2026-06-02 and Assembly 2026-06-03; last action 2026-06-03 'returned to senate'; not delivered to the Governor on 2026-09-29
atoms.instrument: L.2026 S9760/A10182-A (Consumer Debt Uniformity Act)
atoms.condition: An action (not an eviction summary proceeding) against a natural-person former tenant for a residential lease balance, commenced on or after the effective date.
atoms.effect: The action must be commenced within three years. The new CPLR 105(f-1) 'consumer debt' is a purpose test that reaches a residential lease balance, so from that date it displaces NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit for the limitations period, and time-barred status for collectors (NYC:SHIELD-5-77(i); NYC:ADC-20-493.2(b)) is measured on three years. Before that date CPLR 213(2) (six years) governs.
atoms.quote: consumer debt to be commenced within three years. An action arising out

construction.quote: include an obligation or alleged obligation to pay money when sought
This act shall take effect on the ninetieth day after it shall

atoms.reasoning: The bill defines consumer debt by the purpose of the transaction and excludes only obligations sought in an article 7 summary proceeding or secured by real property. A lease balance sued for in an ordinary action falls within it. The act takes effect on its 90th day after becoming law.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 6-A (Good Cause Eviction Law)
atoms.condition: A New York City unit whose monthly rent is greater than 245% of the HUD fair market rent for its county and unit size, as published by DHCR.
atoms.effect: Good Cause Eviction does not apply. The tenancy ends as RPL 226-c and the lease provide, and a tenant who stays after a proper non-renewal owes use and occupancy (NY:RPL-220).
atoms.quote: or two hundred forty-five percent of the fair market rent

judgment_terms: reasonable proportion to the probable loss
atoms.instrument: NY common law of liquidated damages; RPL 227-e (adjudication)
atoms.provision: JMD Holding v Congress Fin.; RPL 227-e; GOL 7-108(1-a)(b)
atoms.condition: The lease fixes a sum payable if the tenant leaves before the term ends (a lease-break or early termination charge, or liquidated damages).
atoms.effect: (a) The sum is owed only if, when the lease was made, it bore a reasonable proportion to the probable loss and the actual loss was difficult to estimate; a sum plainly disproportionate to the probable loss is an unenforceable penalty, and the landlord recovers only proven damages. (b) A clause that makes the tenant pay rent for the rest of the term regardless of re-letting, or otherwise removes the duty to mitigate, is void (NY:RPL-227-e-waiver). (c) An enforceable sum is damages, not rent, damage to the unit, lease utilities or moving and storage, so it is not kept from the deposit and is claimed separately (NY:GOL-7-108(1-a)(b)-refundable). (d) It is not a FARE Act fee (NYC:FARE-damages-rent-not-fees). (e) An NYC lease entered into on or after 2022-06-22 where the tenant left in breach: the landlord recovers no vacating charge, a lease-break sum included, above the fair market cost of preparing the unit for rental, and only with an itemized calculation (NYC:ADC-26-3402-vacating-fee-cap); rent proved under 227-e is outside that ceiling.
atoms.quote: A contractual provision fixing damages in the event of breach will be sustained if the amount liquidated bears a reasonable proportion to the probable loss and the amount of actual loss is incapable or difficult of precise estimation.

construction.quote: If, however, the amount fixed is plainly or grossly disproportionate to the probable loss, the provision calls for a penalty and will not be enforced
Any provision in a lease that exempts a landlord's duty to mitigate damages under this section shall be void as contrary to public policy.

Where a landlord has a duty to mitigate damages, such landlord may not recover from a tenant any amount in excess of the fair market cost necessary to prepare the physical conditions of the premises for rental. In seeking such amount from a tenant, such landlord must provide an itemized list to such tenant demonstrating the calculation of such amount.

atoms.reasoning: JMD Holding is the Court of Appeals test for any liquidated-damages clause. RPL 227-e voids a clause that removes mitigation. The deposit retention list in 7-108(1-a)(b) is closed, and a liquidated sum is none of its four categories.

atoms.instrument: NY General Obligations Law 7-108(1-a) (adjudication)
atoms.condition: The tenant vacated before the lease ended; the unit is under 7-108(1-a).
atoms.effect: The 14-day statement may retain only rent that has fallen due under the lease and is unpaid on the date the statement is sent, including rent that fell due after the tenant left, and only for periods before a new tenant's lease took effect. Rent for periods not yet due may not be held against the deposit; it is claimed later, subject to mitigation and the landlord's burden (NY:RPL-227-e). The rest of the deposit is returned within the 14 days.
atoms.quote: shall return any remaining portion of the deposit to the tenant

construction.quote: plaintiffs remained liable for rent from July 1, 2021 to July 14, 2021, which amount defendant could offset from the security

atoms.reasoning: The statute lets the landlord keep costs due to non-payment of rent and return the rest within 14 days. Rent not yet due has not gone unpaid. Kunik (Appellate Term, 2d Dept) allowed the offset of rent that accrued after vacating up to the day before the new tenant's lease began.

atoms.instrument: NY Abandoned Property Law art. 14 (Justia compilation)
atoms.condition: An unclaimed deposit refund is to be reported to the Comptroller (NY:ABP-1315(2)).
atoms.effect: At least 90 days before the reporting date, mail the tenant a written notice by first-class mail at the address in the landlord's records; if the refund exceeds $1,000, send a second notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, at least 60 days before. Not required where the landlord has no address, or can show its only address is not the tenant's current one (for example the vacated unit); the second notice is not required if the tenant has claimed or the first notice came back undeliverable. The notice says the refund will be reported and paid to the Comptroller unless claimed first. The certified-mail cost may be deducted from the refund as a service charge.
atoms.quote: not less than ninety days prior to the applicable reporting date for such unclaimed property, a written notice by first-class mail

construction.quote: Costs paid to the postal authorities by holders of unclaimed property to provide such written notice by certified mail, return receipt requested, may be deducted from the property as a service charge.

atoms.reasoning: Subdivision 4 allows the certified-mail cost to be deducted from the property.

atoms.instrument: 23 NYCRR Part 1 (DFS debt collection rule; Justia compilation)
atoms.condition: A third-party collector or debt buyer collects a former tenant's lease balance.
atoms.effect: 23 NYCRR Part 1 does not apply: its 'debt' requires a transaction in which credit was extended, and a lease balance is not credit (NY:ADJ-lease-balance-not-consumer-credit). The FDCPA, Regulation F and the city rules apply on their own terms.
atoms.quote: which arises out of a transaction wherein credit has been extended to a consumer

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: An agreement for the occupation of real estate in New York City, oral or written, under which the parties contemplated an occupancy longer than one rental period but did not particularly specify its length ('a long time', 'indefinitely', 'for years' without a valid written term): NY:ADJ-RPL-232-indefinite-term. An agreement that fixes a monthly rent and says nothing about length is presumed month to month and is outside this section (NY:ADJ-RPL-232-monthly-letting). An agreement that states how the occupancy ends is governed by NY:ADJ-RPL-232-agreement-sets-end, and an oral agreement for a stated term longer than one year by NY:ADJ-RPL-232-oral-term-over-one-year.
atoms.effect: The agreement is deemed to continue until the first October 1 after possession began under it. Consequences for the settlement are in NY:ADJ-RPL-232-indefinite-term and NY:ADJ-RPL-232-after-october.
atoms.quote: shall be deemed to continue until the first day of October next after the possession commences under the agreement.

judgment_terms: general letting with a monthly rent reserved
atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7 (adjudication)
atoms.condition: NYC residential occupancy agreement, oral or written, with no fixed end date, that fixes a monthly rent and says nothing about how long the occupancy lasts, or says the letting is 'month to month', 'monthly' or 'by the month'. No proof of a different agreement (such as talk of staying 'a long time': NY:ADJ-RPL-232-indefinite-term).
atoms.effect: The law presumes a month-to-month tenancy from the start; RPL 232 does not apply. The tenant may leave at the end of any monthly term without notice (NY:COMMONLAW-NYC-monthly-tenant-surrender) unless an agreement requires notice (NY:ADJ-NYC-monthly-agreed-notice); the landlord ends it only with the RPL 226-c notice (NY:RPL-232-a). Rent is owed for each month begun and no later month, so nothing after the month in which the tenant leaves may be kept from the deposit or claimed.
atoms.quote: In the absence of contravening proof, the law presumes that where there is a general letting with a monthly rent reserved, an indefinite month-to-month tenancy is created

construction.quote: If nothing had been said concerning the term, and the hiring had been at a certain monthly rent, a tenancy for a month only would have been created.
Moreover, the acceptance of rent on a monthly basis creates a month-to-month tenancy
so a monthly tenant or tenant from month to month may surrender at the end of any month without notice.
see Gerolemou v Soliz
The present bill restores the law substantially as it was previously

atoms.reasoning: Gerolemou (Appellate Term, 2d Dept, 2000), cited by the First Department in 2025 (Olympic Galleria), presumes a month-to-month tenancy from a general letting at a monthly rent. Spies, the authority for RPL 232's reach, says the same and applied the statute only because the parties spoke of a long stay. T.I.B. (App Term 1st, affirmed) treats a monthly tenant as free to leave at any month end. Stauber does not decide the point: its sublet began in September, so the statute and the monthly-acceptance rule gave the same result, and it relied on both. The 1920 amendment restored the prior law, which includes the Spies and Gilfoyle constructions. Gerolemou and T.I.B. prevail on the bare monthly rent.

judgment_terms: parties contemplated a longer occupation than one rental period
reasonable and customary steps to rent
atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7 (adjudication)
atoms.condition: NYC residential occupancy agreement, oral or written, under which the parties contemplated an occupancy longer than one rental period without fixing its length ('a long time', 'indefinitely', 'for years' without a valid written term), that does not state how the occupancy ends (NY:ADJ-RPL-232-agreement-sets-end). The tenant leaves before the first October 1 after possession began. A monthly rent with nothing said about length is not this case (NY:ADJ-RPL-232-monthly-letting).
atoms.effect: RPL 232 applies, whether or not rent is fixed and paid monthly. The term runs to the first October 1 after possession began and binds both parties. A tenant who leaves earlier without the landlord's acceptance of a surrender owes rent through September 30 of that year, as damages subject to the landlord's duty to re-rent and its burden (NY:RPL-227-e). On the 14-day statement the deposit covers only rent already due and unpaid (NY:ADJ-early-departure-rent-retention); later rent is a separate claim. After that October 1 the monthly rules apply (NY:ADJ-RPL-232-after-october).
atoms.quote: But in the present case the parties contemplated a longer occupation than a month

construction.quote: The fact that the rent was fixed at $58 a month, and was payable monthly, does not affect the question, as the statute includes cases where the agreement provides how and when the rent shall be payable.
It was clear from that enactment that when land was occupied by a tenant without a fixed period of letting having been agreed upon, the period terminated May first.
who failed to secure written leases and who, therefore, under the law as it then existed were only monthly tenants for the purpose of securing increased rents.
The lease term did not specify an ending date but inserted the word indefinitely.

atoms.reasoning: Spies applied the statute to an open stay because the parties contemplated a longer occupation than a month (the tenant said she would stay 'a long time, for five years or eight years'); the monthly rent did not take it outside the statute. Abbey (Sup Ct Kings 2006) applied RPL 232 to a written lease 'indefinitely'. Souhami reads the older text the same way for a stay without a fixed period. Whether the parties contemplated a longer stay is a finding on the words used. The statutory date was May 1 until 1918 and is October 1 since L.1920 c.130.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7 (adjudication)
atoms.condition: An NYC tenancy whose term was fixed by RPL 232 (NY:ADJ-RPL-232-indefinite-term), where the tenant stayed past the first October 1 after possession began and the landlord accepted rent for a later period.
atoms.effect: The tenancy continues month to month. From that October 1 the monthly rules govern the ending and the rent owed (NY:COMMONLAW-NYC-monthly-tenant-surrender, NY:ADJ-NYC-monthly-agreed-notice, NY:RPL-232-a); RPL 232 does not renew the term to the next October 1. So RPL 232 changes the settlement only for a tenant who leaves before the first October 1 of the occupancy.
atoms.quote: The acceptance of rent thereafter creates a month-to-month tenancy, pursuant to section 232-c of the Real Property Law.

construction.quote: the tenancy created by the acceptance of such rent shall be a tenancy from month to month commencing on the first day after the expiration of such term.
Thus, by any legal definition, plaintiffs’ occupancy of the apartment involved a month-to-month subtenancy.
after October 1, 1924, the tenant held over from year to year down to October 1, 1929
Thereafter, Nigel became a month-to-month tenant by continuing to pay monthly for the exclusive use of the basement apartment.

atoms.reasoning: Before RPL 232-c, a tenant holding over after a yearly statutory term could be held for another year (Norriv Realty, App Term 1930). RPL 232-c, the later statute, makes a holdover after any term longer than one month a month-to-month tenancy when rent is accepted, and Stauber (1st Dept) and Adina apply it to a term that ended under RPL 232. A statutory term of one month or less (possession in September) reaches the same result by the monthly acceptance of rent (Stauber). Norriv shows the rule before RPL 232-c (a holdover after the statutory term renewed from year to year). Hyacinth Green (Civ Ct Kings 2025) applies the current rule: after the first October 1 the occupant paying monthly is a month-to-month tenant. This covers an agreement at a monthly rent with no agreed period (NY:ADJ-RPL-232-indefinite-term).

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7 (adjudication)
atoms.provision: RPL 232; agreement that fixes its own ending
atoms.condition: An NYC occupancy agreement without a fixed end date that states how the occupancy ends, for example that either party may end it on a stated number of days' notice, or that it continues until either party ends it on notice.
atoms.effect: The agreement's own ending mechanism governs; RPL 232 does not cut the occupancy off at October 1 and does not bind the tenant to stay until then. Rent runs until the occupancy ends as the agreement provides, subject to NY:RPL-227-e when the tenant leaves without the agreed notice.
atoms.quote: the lower courts erred in applying Real Property Law § 232 — a statute of limited purpose and application — to limit either the Comptroller’s authority or the contract’s terms.

construction.quote: The agreement approved by the Comptroller included an initial fixed term and the option to continue the occupancy thereafter for so long as the parties mutually desired, terminable by either without penalty on 45 days’ written notice.

atoms.reasoning: The Court of Appeals (City of New York v State, 87 NY2d 982) held that RPL 232, 'a statute of limited purpose and application', does not override an occupancy agreement that continues until either party ends it on notice. That decision controls over Adina 74 Realty (Civil Court 1980), which applied RPL 232 to a letter agreement with 30-day notice terms: the Court of Appeals is higher and later.

atoms.instrument: NY Multiple Dwelling Law (adjudication)
atoms.condition: The unit is in a house certified or built as a one- or two-family dwelling that contains an illegal unit (for example a basement or cellar apartment, or a second unit in a one-family house) or has no certificate of occupancy for the use, and the building is not occupied as the home of three or more families (NY:MDL-4(7)-multiple-dwelling).
atoms.effect: No statute bars rent. The owner may recover rent and use and occupancy for the months the tenant occupied, keep the deposit for it on the 14-day statement, and sue for it; the Multiple Dwelling Law forfeitures (NY:MDL-302(1)(b), NY:MDL-325(2)) reach only multiple dwellings. If the house is actually occupied by three or more families it is a multiple dwelling and NY:MDL-302(1)(b) bars rent for the period. An illegal occupancy remains exposed to a vacate order (NY:ADJ-vacate-order-rent) and to the one- or two-family registration stay (NYC:ADC-27-2107(b)-rent-stay).
atoms.quote: there is no bar to the recovery of rent when a dwelling that has a certificate of occupancy as a one-family dwelling contains an illegal apartment. It is only in the Multiple Dwelling Law that the Legislature has seen fit to impose a forfeiture of rent as a penalty.

construction.quote: which are to be strictly construed
there was no proof that the house constituted a multiple dwelling
is occupied as the residence or home of three or more families living independently of each other.

atoms.reasoning: The Appellate Term, Second Department (Pickering v Chappe, 29 Misc 3d 6, reversing a Civil Court award of the deposit; followed in Thomas v Brown) holds that the rent forfeitures are confined to multiple dwellings and strictly construed, and binds Kings, Queens and Richmond, where most one- and two-family rentals are. The strict-construction rule it applies is the Appellate Term, First Department's own (Goho Equities; Coulston, both cited in Pickering), and no First Department court holds otherwise, so the rule is the same in New York and Bronx Counties. Civil Court decisions that denied rent for illegal apartments in one-family houses (Fazio v Kelly) were rejected by Pickering.

judgment_terms: owner bound wholly or in part to correct the conditions
atoms.instrument: NY common law of eviction (adjudication); NYC Admin. Code 27-2142
atoms.condition: The unit is vacated under a government vacate order (HPD under Admin. Code 27-2139, the Department of Buildings or the Fire Department) issued because of conditions or an unlawful occupancy that the owner was bound, wholly or in part, to correct or avoid.
atoms.effect: No rent or use and occupancy is recovered for any period after the tenant had to leave, while the order stands or after the tenant surrenders; nor may the deposit be kept for it. An installment that fell due before the order is owed as an installment, but a tenant who vacated because of the ouster recovers the per-day share covering the days after it, on failure of consideration: on the move-out account the landlord charges or keeps only the share up to and including the day of the ouster and refunds or credits the rest (subject to NY:RPL-235-b for the earned part). Because the owner was at fault, the tenant also has a damages claim for the value of the rest of the term less the rent reserved, which offsets any landlord claim. A tenant that keeps possession of any part recovers no proportionate share. If the order resulted only from conditions the tenant or its household caused (Admin. Code 27-2006), the order is no defense and the lease governs. Where the order follows sudden physical injury to the building (fire, collapse, flood or a kindred casualty), NY:RPL-227 governs and reaches the same adjustment by statute.
atoms.quote: the landlord cannot recover any rent for the period after the eviction occurred.

construction.quote: No person shall occupy, or cause or permit to be occupied, any dwelling or part thereof while such dwelling or part is subject to a vacate order.
I am led to the conclusion that section 227 of the Real Property Law has no application
be responsible for violations of this code to the extent that he or she has the power to prevent the occurrence of a violation.
In the case of actual eviction, even where the tenant is only partially evicted, liability for all rent is suspended
constitutes a danger to the life, health, or safety of its occupants, shall be deemed to be unfit for human habitation.
The order shall require all persons occupying the dwelling or part affected to vacate it within a period of time
it was no defense to the rent which had become due in advance September first

If by reason of the eviction plaintiff had vacated the premises she would have been entitled to recover the proportionate part of the rent paid in advance for the balance of the month of September on the ground of failure of consideration
but her retention of possession to the end of the term prevents any such recovery.
This would be so if the breach of the covenants for quiet enjoyment resulted from the fault of Strasburger.

atoms.reasoning: The Appellate Division, First Department (Younger v Campbell, 1917) held that a tenant ousted by a government vacate order that followed, even in part, from the landlord's failure to do work that was its own obligation owes no rent after the ouster; the trial court below had held RPL 227 inapplicable to vacate orders, which leaves the eviction rule as the governing law. The Housing Maintenance Code forbids anyone to occupy a unit under a vacate order, so there is no lawful use to pay for. Under Barash (Court of Appeals) an eviction attributable to the landlord suspends rent. The tenant-fault branch follows the code's allocation of violations the tenant causes (27-2006). Admin. Code 27-2139 and 27-2140 give HPD the vacate power for any dwelling or part unfit for habitation and make the order require every occupant to leave, which is the ouster Younger treats as an eviction. Kennedy v Peterart (App Term 1st Dept 1939) holds the eviction no defense to rent already due in advance but lets a tenant who vacated because of it recover the proportionate part for the rest of the period; Matter of Strasburger (Court of Appeals 1892) gives the full loss of bargain where the lessor is at fault. Younger is consistent: there the eviction preceded the due date.

judgment_terms: substantially and materially deprive the tenant of the beneficial use and enjoyment
atoms.instrument: NY common law of eviction
atoms.condition: The departing tenant claims it left because of the landlord's wrongful acts or failures (for example no heat or water, persistent leaks, lockout), or the landlord excluded the tenant from all or part of the unit.
atoms.effect: Constructive eviction: where the landlord's wrongful acts substantially and materially deprived the tenant of the beneficial use and enjoyment of the unit and the tenant abandoned possession because of them, no rent is owed after the abandonment, and no lease-break or re-letting claim lies for the rest of the term. A tenant who stayed cannot claim it. Actual eviction: where the landlord physically ousted or excluded the tenant from all or part of the unit (lockout, lock change, taking a room), all rent is suspended for the period, even though the tenant kept the rest. For conditions short of either, rent is offset by the habitability warranty (NY:RPL-235-b).
atoms.quote: constructive eviction exists where, although there has been no physical expulsion or exclusion of the tenant, the landlord's wrongful acts substantially and materially deprive the tenant of the beneficial use and enjoyment of the premises

construction.quote: The tenant, however, must abandon possession in order to claim that there was a constructive eviction
An actual eviction occurs only when the landlord wrongfully ousts the tenant from physical possession of the leased premises.
In the case of actual eviction, even where the tenant is only partially evicted, liability for all rent is suspended

atoms.reasoning: Barash (Court of Appeals) states both doctrines and their conditions. A tenant's obligation to pay rent is dependent on the landlord's not evicting it; after a constructive eviction and abandonment there is no continuing tenancy from which rent or re-letting damages could run.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 7
atoms.condition: During the tenancy the tenant lawfully paid a gas, electric, steam or water provider for service the landlord was responsible for and failed to pay (PSL 33, 34, 116 or the water provisions named in the section).
atoms.effect: The payment is deductible from rent. On the move-out account it is credited against any rent claimed; rent is not due to the extent of the payment. An owner of a multiple dwelling whose non-payment caused a discontinuance is also liable to the tenant for compensatory and punitive damages, which offset a rent claim.
atoms.quote: such payment shall be deductible from any future payment of rent.

construction.quote: shall be liable for compensatory and punitive damages to any tenant whose utility service is so discontinued.

atoms.reasoning: Subdivision 1 makes the payment a deduction from rent; the account that states the rent owed must apply it. Subdivision 2 creates a damages claim for a multiple-dwelling tenant, which the tenant may set off against the landlord's claim.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Actions and Proceedings Law art. 7-A
atoms.condition: An NYC dwelling is under a 7-A judgment appointing an administrator (tenant or HPD proceeding under RPAPL 769-770) and the departing tenant owed rent for a period after the judgment was entered (petitioning tenant) or served on it (other tenants).
atoms.effect: That rent is payable to the administrator, who demands, collects and sues for it. The owner's right to collect it is void to the extent the tenant deposited it with the administrator, and deposit with the administrator is a defense to any claim for it. The owner and its manager may not collect that rent or keep the deposit for it; an unpaid balance for those months is reported to the administrator. Rent for earlier periods and non-rent charges stay the owner's. The administrator, as a court appointee, needs no broker licence (RPL 442-f).
atoms.quote: shall be void and unenforceable to the extent that such petitioning or non-petitioning tenant, as the case may be, has deposited such moneys with the administrator in accordance with the terms of such judgment

construction.quote: any rents to become due in the future from all tenants occupying such dwelling shall be deposited with such administrator as they fall due
to demand, collect and receive the rents from the tenants; and to institute all necessary legal proceedings

One-third or more of the tenants occupying a dwelling located in the city of New York or the commissioner of the department of the city of New York charged with enforcement of the housing maintenance code
may be maintained in the civil court of the city of New York

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 12-A
atoms.condition: A person or business, for another and for a fee, commission or other valuable consideration, collects, offers to collect or attempts to collect rent for the use of real estate in New York: it demands rent, receives rent payments, or applies money it holds (such as the deposit) to rent. Rent includes a former tenant's unpaid rent for months of the tenancy and rent reserved by the lease for months after an early departure. The collector is not the owner or the owner's employee (NY:ADJ-broker-owner-and-staff), is not exempt (NY:RPL-442-f-exemptions), and the collection is not a mere incidental feature of services whose subject is something other than real estate.
atoms.effect: It is acting as a real estate broker and must hold a New York broker's licence before doing so (an individual working for a licensed broker holds a salesperson or associate broker licence). Rent owed for the tenancy stays rent after the tenant moves out, so collecting a move-out rent balance is collecting rent. Not collecting rent, and needing no broker licence: collecting only charges other than the periodic rent for the unit (damage, late fees, utilities, a fixed lease-break sum), even if the lease calls them additional rent; collecting use and occupancy owed for occupancy after the tenancy ended (NY:RPL-220); preparing statements, computing the account or inspecting without demanding, receiving or applying rent money; refunding the tenant's own deposit. Calling the service by another name (finder, coordinator, platform) does not change the act. Consequences: NY:RPL-442-d-442-e-unlicensed.

atoms.reasoning: The definition turns on the act: collecting, or offering or attempting to collect, rent for another for a fee. The words carry no time limit, so rent that fell due during the tenancy is still 'rent for the use of real estate' when it is collected after move-out, and reading it so applies the words rather than extending them. Article 12-A is penal and strictly construed (Weingast, Court of Appeals; Kreuter, 2d Dept), which keeps out what the words do not name: charges that are not rent for the use of the unit, and use and occupancy, which the Real Property Law names separately as 'reasonable compensation for the use and occupation' (RPL 220), owed after the tenancy has ended. The Department of State draws the same line for management companies: collecting rent requires the licence; strictly maintenance does not, because the company is not handling another person's money. The incidental-feature rule (Weingast; Dodge v Richmond, 1st Dept; Eaton, 2d Dept) spares services whose subject is something else, such as the sale of a business or a financing plan, where the real-estate act is a by-product; it does not spare rent collection within services for a rental property, which the Second Department held required the licence (Fields v Pinkney, 2025), and a new label does not help (Futersak, 2d Dept).

atoms.effect: Each act is a misdemeanor; the Department of State may investigate. The collector cannot recover compensation for the services of which rent collection is part, and where the brokerage element is the dominant feature of the engagement the whole agreement is unenforceable. It is liable to a penalty of one to four times the compensation it received, recoverable by any person aggrieved. The owner's claim against the former tenant is unaffected, and the tenant's payment to the owner's authorized agent discharges the tenant. Which services form the tainted part is a judgment on the engagement's terms.

The penalties run against the unlicensed agent; nothing in article 12-A voids the tenant's lease obligation or the owner's claim. Futersak (2d Dept 2011, reversing the Supreme Court decision of 2010) applies the fee bar whatever the service is called. The 2010 Supreme Court decision holding otherwise was reversed and decides nothing. G.C. atoms.reasoning: Section 440(3) defines a salesperson as one who collects rent for or on behalf of a broker, so a broker's rent-collecting staff need the salesperson licence. The Department of State counts 'managing property owned by your employer' as unlicensed general real estate experience, which confirms that an owner's employees are outside the licensing requirement; and its unlicensed-assistant guidance limits unlicensed broker staff to activities not listed in section 440. The text confirms the employee rule: the Legislature brought an owner's salaried employees within the definition ('shall also include') only for article 9-A lot sales, which shows that an owner's salaried employees are otherwise outside it (Colon, Court of Appeals). A separate company, even one affiliated with the owner, that collects the owner's rent for a fee acts for another and is within RPL 440(1).

atoms.condition: Configuration 1: Handoff, for a fee from the owner or manager, does any of these for a rent balance (including a move-out rent balance): demands it from the tenant or former tenant in its own name or through its own staff's letters, calls or messages; receives rent payments into an account it controls; or holds the deposit and applies it to rent or remits the rent part to the owner.
atoms.effect: Handoff is acting as a real estate broker and must hold a New York broker's licence (the company, through a licensed representative broker, with its rent-collecting staff licensed as salespersons or associate brokers) before it does so. The collection is not an incidental feature of another service: Handoff's engagement is the rental unit and the tenancy, and collecting rent is itself the licensed act. Without the licence, NY:RPL-442-d-442-e-unlicensed applies, including loss of compensation for the services of which rent collection is part, the whole engagement where brokerage is its dominant feature, and a penalty of up to four times its compensation recoverable by any person aggrieved. Collecting only non-rent charges does not require the licence (NY:RPL-440(1)-rent-collection).

atoms.reasoning: Handoff would collect rent for another for a fee, which is the statutory act. The incidental-feature rule applies where the real-estate act is a by-product of services about something else: a financing plan (Eaton) or the sale of a business (Weingast, Dodge v Richmond). Handoff's services concern the rental unit and its tenancy, and resolving the tenancy's money, of which rent is the main item, is one of its two outcomes, so real estate is the principal element (Dodge). The Second Department refused to treat rent collection within property-management services as incidental (Fields, 2025), and the Department of State requires the licence of a management company that collects rent.

atoms.instrument: NY Real Property Law art. 12-A applied to Handoff configurations
atoms.condition: Configuration 2: Handoff inspects, builds the account, prepares the itemized statement and any balance letter, and instructs the refund; the owner or its licensed manager holds the deposit, applies it to any rent, makes any demand for a rent balance in its own name, and receives any payment into its own account. Handoff may send the statement and refund if the statement accounts for the deposit without demanding payment of a rent balance.
atoms.effect: No broker licence is required: Handoff neither collects nor attempts to collect rent. Handoff is in Configuration 1 (NY:HANDOFF-broker-config-collects-rent) for any act by which it (a) holds the deposit or a tenant payment in an account it controls and applies or remits it as rent, (b) demands a rent balance from the tenant, in anyone's name, by a letter it sends or by its staff's calls or messages, or (c) receives rent as the owner's agent. A payment link that settles the tenant's payment directly into the owner's or licensed manager's account, without Handoff taking custody, is the owner's collection. Refunding the tenant's own deposit is not collecting rent.

The listed acts are collecting, offering or attempting to collect: taking custody of rent money, applying held money to rent, and demanding payment are those acts whoever's letterhead is used, because the sender is the one attempting to collect. The Department of State's line is custody of another person's money; a payment that never passes through Handoff's control is received by the owner.

atoms.condition: Configuration 3: Handoff's people work as salaried agents of a licensed broker (for example the manager's brokerage) and collect rent for it.
atoms.effect: Each individual who collects or attempts to collect rent must hold a salesperson or associate broker licence associated with that broker; unlicensed individuals may do only clerical work under the broker's supervision. Handoff as a company is not a salesperson: if the company itself contracts with the broker to collect rent for a fee, it acts for another for a fee and needs its own broker licence (Configuration 1). The broker must supervise each such salesperson by regular, frequent and consistent personal guidance, including the collection work, and broker and salesperson keep records of each transaction (NY:19NYCRR-175.21-broker-supervision); without that supervision the association RPL 441(1)(d) requires is not met.

atoms.condition: NYC residential tenant took possession under an oral agreement (nothing in writing subscribed by the landlord or its authorized agent) for a stated term longer than one year, for example 'two years' or 'thirteen months', and pays rent monthly.
atoms.effect: The agreement is void as a lease, and RPL 232 does not apply because the parties did specify a duration. The tenant who entered and pays monthly rent is a month-to-month tenant from the start and is not bound to stay for the stated term. The NYC monthly rules govern the ending and the rent owed: the tenant may surrender at the end of any monthly term without notice, owing rent for each month begun (NY:COMMONLAW-NYC-monthly-tenant-surrender); the landlord ends it with the RPL 226-c notice (NY:RPL-232-a).

atoms.reasoning: GOL 5-703(2) voids an unwritten lease for more than one year. The Court of Appeals (People ex rel. Botsford v Darling, 1872) holds that entry and monthly payment under such a void agreement create a month-to-month tenancy, and the Court of Common Pleas (Geiger v Braun, 1876) applied it in New York City, holding that the city duration statute (now RPL 232) does not apply because the parties fixed a time, and that the tenant is not bound to stay for the void term. Geiger also held, extending Darling, that such a tenant must give a month's notice to quit. That part is not the law today: Darling decided a landlord's removal of the tenant, a notice now governed by RPL 232-a; for a tenant leaving, the Appellate Term, First Department (T.I.B. Corp. v Repetto, affirmed by the Appellate Division, leave to appeal denied) holds that a New York City monthly tenant may surrender at the end of any month without notice. T.I.B. is later and from a higher court than Geiger, and the Legislature's one-month tenant notice in RPL 232-b applies only outside the city (NY:COMMONLAW-NYC-monthly-tenant-surrender).
